paragraphs.context: The moon would be black tonight, and they had jiggered the watches
paragraphs.mainIdea: Chett's mutiny plan is ready; tonight is the night.
paragraphs.simple: The night will be very dark. Chett and his men have fixed the guard turns so their own men stand watch. The wildlings may come any day, so Chett wants to run away before that. He wants to live.

paragraphs.context: The plan was Chett's. He was the clever one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Chett lays out the full mutiny plan: who to kill, how, and where to flee.
paragraphs.simple: This was Chett's plan. He was the smart one. He used to work for Maester Aemon until Jon Snow took his job. Tonight he will kill Sam, set the ravens free so no messages reach the Wall, and his men will quietly kill the officers. They have hidden food and horses ready. With Mormont dead, old Ser Ottyn will run back to the Wall and no one will chase them.

paragraphs.context: The wildlings are on the march, following the course of the Milkwater
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont warns the Watch that a huge wildling host is coming down the Milkwater.
paragraphs.simple: The wildlings are marching down out of the mountains along the Milkwater river. Their best fighters are in front with Harma Dogshead. Most of them walk, have poor weapons, and carry women, children, animals, and all they own. They are many but weak, and they do not know the Watch is here.

paragraphs.context: We'll hit hard and be away before their horsemen can form up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Smallwood explains the attack plan: strike fast, then run.
paragraphs.simple: They will hit the wildlings hard and leave before the enemy horsemen can get ready. If chased, they will run, turn, and hit again further down. They will burn wagons, scatter animals, and kill as many as they can, even Mance Rayder. If the wildlings run home, the Watch wins. If not, they will harass them all the way to the Wall.

paragraphs.context: The Lannister blood runs thin in this one.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime explains who Ser Cleos is and why he is unimpressive.
paragraphs.simple: Cleos is Jaime's aunt's son. His father Emmon Frey married into the Lannisters and always feared Lord Tywin. Cleos looks like a weasel, fights badly, and is cowardly. Lady Stark promised to free him if he carries her message, and he vowed to do it.

paragraphs.context: Downriver, the rising sun shimmered against the wind-whipped surface of the river.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riverlands show the marks of war as they sail past.
paragraphs.simple: Down the river, the sun shone on the rough water. The south shore was smooth red clay. Small streams joined the river. The north shore was wild, with high rocky cliffs and trees. Jaime saw an empty old watchtower covered in climbing roses.

paragraphs.context: But the war had taken its toll.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The war has emptied the riverlands.
paragraphs.simple: But the war had done its damage. They sailed past villages with no people in them. A torn empty fishing net was the only sign of fishermen. A girl ran away when she saw their sail. Later they passed peasants digging under a burned tower. The men looked at them with dull eyes and went back to work once they saw the boat was no danger.

paragraphs.context: Could there have been another woman in her father's life?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn wonders who 'Tansy' is — a secret woman from her father's past?
paragraphs.simple: Could her father have had another woman in his life? A village girl he wronged when young? Or a serving girl after her mother died? The thought upset her. Suddenly she felt she had never known her father at all.

paragraphs.context: Could Tansy be some pet name he called Lysa
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn considers that Tansy might be Lysa, and that Lysa lost a child.
paragraphs.simple: Could Tansy be a pet name for Lysa, like Cat is for Catelyn? Her father had mistaken her for Lysa before. He said 'You'll have others. Sweet babes, and trueborn.' Lysa had lost five babies. But never at Riverrun, where Father could comfort her. Unless she was with child that first time, long ago.

paragraphs.context: Father, I know what you did.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn realizes her father forced Lysa to abort a pregnancy so Jon Arryn would marry her.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn stood over her dying father. 'Father, I know what you did.' She was no longer an innocent bride. She was a widow, a traitor, a grieving mother, wise in the ways of the world. 'You made him take her,' she whispered. 'Lysa was the price Jon Arryn had to pay for the swords and spears of House Tully.'

paragraphs.context: The next day, as she broke her fast, Catelyn asked for quill and paper
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn writes to Lysa begging her to forgive their dying father.
paragraphs.simple: The next day at breakfast, Catelyn wrote to her sister Lysa in the Vale. She told of Bran and Rickon, but mostly of their father. His thoughts are all of the wrong he did Lysa, now that he is dying. The maester dare not make his pain medicine stronger. It is time for Father to rest, yet he fights on. He needs Lysa's forgiveness. She begs Lysa to come, or at least write a few loving words so he might die in peace.

paragraphs.context: She was only ten, a skinny girl on a stolen horse
paragraphs.mainIdea: Despite the danger, Arya feels strangely calm, remembering Syrio's words.
paragraphs.simple: She knew she should be more afraid. She was only ten, a thin girl on a stolen horse, with a dark forest ahead and men behind who would cut off her feet. Yet she felt calmer than ever. The rain had washed the blood off her hands, she wore a sword, wolves moved in the dark, and Arya Stark was not afraid. 'Fear cuts deeper than swords,' she whispered, as Syrio had taught her.

paragraphs.context: threading their way carefully between the shells of blackened hovels
paragraphs.mainIdea: They ride through a burned village of hanged men; Arya says her death prayer.
paragraphs.simple: They rode carefully through a burned village, between ruined houses and past a dozen dead men hanging from apple trees. When Hot Pie saw them he prayed to the Mother over and over. Arya looked at the dead and said her own prayer — her list of names: Ser Gregor, Dunsen, Polliver, Raff the Sweetling, the Tickler and the Hound, Ser Ilyn, Ser Meryn, King Joffrey, Queen Cersei. She ended with 'valar morghulis,' touched Jaqen's coin, and plucked an apple from among the dead men as she rode under them.

paragraphs.context: She would make much better time on her own, Arya knew
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya refuses to abandon Hot Pie and Gendry.
paragraphs.simple: She knew she would travel much faster alone, but she could not leave them. They were her pack, her friends, the only living friends she had left. Without her they would still be safe at Harrenhal. If the Mummers catch them, she plans to say she is Ned Stark's daughter and command them to take her to her brother and not harm the boys. But they might not believe her.

paragraphs.context: Lord Tywin had wasted little time.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin is already erasing Tyrion: he took the Tower of the Hand and knighted Bronn himself.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin had not waited at all. Moving Tyrion out of the Tower of the Hand to take it himself was a message anyone could understand, and knighting Bronn by his own command was another. Tyrion had promised Bronn the knighthood, not his father.

paragraphs.context: They tied her to a post in the yard and scourged her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion learns Cersei had Alayaya whipped and thrown out naked.
paragraphs.simple: They tied Alayaya to a post in the yard and whipped her, then threw her out of the gate naked and bloody. Tyrion thought absurdly that she had been learning to read. Alayaya was a whore, but a sweet, brave, innocent girl. Tyrion had never touched her; she was only a cover to hide Shae. He had never thought what the role might cost her.

paragraphs.context: Is it true that Stannis was put to rout by Renly's ghost?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion hears that 'Renly's ghost' routed Stannis's army.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion asked if Stannis was really beaten by Renly's ghost. Bronn said that from the towers they only saw banners in the mud and men throwing down spears to run. But hundreds in taverns and brothels swear they saw Lord Renly kill men himself. Most of Stannis's army had been Renly's first, and they went back to him at the sight of the green armor.

paragraphs.context: You are an ill-made, devious, disobedient, spiteful little creature
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin brutally rejects Tyrion and denies him Casterly Rock forever.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin called Tyrion an ill-made, lying, disobedient, spiteful little creature full of envy, lust, and low cunning. The law lets Tyrion bear the Lannister name only because Tywin cannot prove he is not his son. But neither gods nor men will ever make Tywin let Tyrion turn Casterly Rock into his whorehouse.

paragraphs.context: Thirst; hunger; exposure. They were his companions
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos names his killers — thirst, hunger, cold — and accepts dying at sea.
paragraphs.simple: Thirst, hunger, and cold were his companions, with him every hour. In time he thought of them as friends. Soon one of them would pity him and free him. Or he would walk into the water and swim for a shore he knew was north, too far for his weak body, but that did not matter. He had always been a sailor; he was meant to die at sea.

paragraphs.context: And then some vast beast had let out a roar
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos remembers the wildfire destroying the fleet.
paragraphs.simple: Then a vast beast seemed to roar, and green flames were everywhere: wildfire. Matthos stood at Davos's elbow when the ship seemed to lift from the water. Davos was thrown into the river, spinning in the current. Upstream the flames tore fifty feet into the sky. He saw Black Betha and Fury burning, and burning men jumping into the water to drown. Ahead was the great iron chain across the river, and nothing but burning ships and wildfire from bank to bank.

paragraphs.context: You rowed her into Storm's End in the black of night
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos confesses his own guilt in Melisandre's crimes.
paragraphs.simple: 'It was her work,' Davos said, 'and yours, onion knight. You rowed her into Storm's End in the black of night, so she could release her shadow child. You are not guiltless. You sailed under her banner. You watched the Seven burn at Dragonstone and did nothing. She gave the Father's justice and the Mother's mercy to the fire, and you held your tongue. Even when she killed old Maester Cressen, you did nothing.'

paragraphs.context: Stannis lives, he knew then. I have a king still.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos realizes the ship is friendly and finds a reason to live.
paragraphs.simple: The galley might be Joffrey's, he realized. If he said the wrong name, they would leave him. But no, her hull was striped — she was Lysene, Salladhor Saan's ship. The Mother had sent her. Stannis lives, he knew then. He still had a king. And other sons, and a loyal loving wife. How could he have forgotten? The Mother was merciful indeed.

paragraphs.context: I wish the Hound were here.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa regrets refusing the Hound and keeps his cloak.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa wished the Hound were here. On the night of the battle, Sandor Clegane had come to take her from the city, but she refused. Sometimes she lay awake wondering if she was wise. She had hidden his bloody white cloak in a chest under her summer clothes. She could not say why she kept it. Men said the Hound turned coward in the battle, but Sansa understood — it was only fire he feared.

paragraphs.context: You Starks were kings once, the Arryns and the Lannisters as well
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olenna explains why the Tyrells backed Renly and must now see it through.
paragraphs.simple: Olenna said the Starks, Arryns, and Lannisters were all kings once, but the Tyrells were only stewards until Aegon the Dragon burned the true King of the Reach. Even their claim to Highgarden is weak. But her son Mace wants to see his grandson on the Iron Throne. They should never have joined this folly, but what is done is done. After Mace crowned Renly, they were in it up to their knees, so now they must finish it.

paragraphs.context: It is easy to mount a lion and not so easy to get off
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olenna warns that allying with the Lannisters is dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: Olenna said her oaf son is now doing what her husband did — only he is riding a lion, not a horse. It is easy to climb onto a lion and hard to get off, she warned him, but he only chuckles. A lion is not a pet cat, she told him. Kings would do better to put down their swords and listen to their mothers.

paragraphs.context: A monster, she whispered, so tremulously she could scarcely hear her own voice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa finally tells the truth: Joffrey is a monster.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa felt her heart in her throat. The Queen of Thorns was so close Sansa could smell her sour breath. 'A monster,' Sansa whispered, so shakily she could hardly hear herself. 'Joffrey is a monster. He lied about the butcher's boy and made Father kill my wolf. When I displease him, he has the Kingsguard beat me. He's evil and cruel, my lady, it's so. And the queen as well.'

paragraphs.context: There were more fires than Jon Snow could count, hundreds of fires, thousands
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon sees the vast wildling host camped along the Milkwater.
paragraphs.simple: The world was grey dark, smelling of pine and cold. Mists rose as the riders moved through stones and trees, down toward fires spread like jewels across the river valley. There were more fires than Jon could count — hundreds, thousands — a second river of lights along the icy white Milkwater.

paragraphs.context: There were cookfires all along the river, amongst wayns and carts and sleds.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon sees the wildling camp is full of families, not just fighters.
paragraphs.simple: Cookfires lined the river among carts and sleds. Many wildlings had raised tents of hide and wool. Others slept under rocks or wagons. At one fire a man hardened spear points. Two youths sparred with staffs. A dozen women sat fletching arrows. But not all was warlike — women danced, a baby cried, a boy ran playing, sheep and goats wandered, oxen searched for grass.

paragraphs.context: The camp goes on forever, he reflected, but it's more a hundred camps than one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon judges the wildling camp has numbers but no discipline.
paragraphs.simple: Jon had never seen so many wildlings. The camp went on forever, but it was more like a hundred camps than one, each more open to attack than the last. Stretched over long miles, they had almost no defenses — no pits or sharp stakes, only small patrols. Each group had simply stopped where it liked. If his brothers caught them so scattered, many would pay for that freedom with their lives. They had numbers, but the Watch had discipline, and in battle discipline beats numbers.

paragraphs.context: The black wool cloak of a Sworn Brother of the Night's Watch
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mance explains he deserted over a cloak.
paragraphs.simple: Mance said it was for his cloak. Once on a ranging they killed a great elk. A shadowcat, drawn by the smell of blood, shredded Mance's cloak — and his arm and back too. A wildling healer's daughter sewed the tears with precious red silk from Asshai. But at the Shadow Tower they gave him a new plain black cloak and told him the old one was fit for burning. So he left the next morning — for a place where a man could wear any cloak he chose.

paragraphs.context: The first time they had done it, she feared that they meant to kill each other
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany watches her dragons play-fight in the sky.
paragraphs.simple: Dragons like to attack from above, Dany had learned. If one got between the other and the sun, he would fold his wings and dive screaming, and they would fall from the sky locked together, jaws snapping and tails lashing. The first time, she feared they meant to kill each other, but it was only play. As soon as they hit the sea they broke apart and rose again, hissing, steam rising off them.

paragraphs.context: however strong or fast or skilled a knight may be, there are others who can match him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Whitebeard says no warrior is unbeatable; luck decides battles.
paragraphs.simple: Whitebeard said he had seen a hundred tournaments and more wars than he wished. However strong, fast, or skilled a knight may be, others can match him. A man wins one tourney and loses the next quickly. A slippery patch of grass can mean defeat, or what he ate the night before. A change in the wind can bring victory.

paragraphs.context: Until one day Prince Rhaegar found something in his scrolls that changed him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Whitebeard tells how the bookish Rhaegar suddenly became a warrior.
paragraphs.simple: As a boy, Prince Rhaegar loved books too much. He learned to read so early men joked his mother swallowed books while pregnant. He cared nothing for children's games. The maesters admired his mind, but the knights joked sourly. Then one day he found something in his scrolls that changed him. No one knows what. The boy appeared in the yard one morning and told the master-at-arms, 'I will require sword and armor. It seems I must be a warrior.'

paragraphs.context: Eighteen times the Dothraki charged, and broke themselves on those shields and spears
paragraphs.mainIdea: Three thousand Unsullied defeat a huge Dothraki horde.
paragraphs.simple: The Dothraki charged. The Unsullied locked shields, lowered spears, and stood firm. Eighteen times the Dothraki charged and broke on those shields like waves on rock. Three times Temmo sent archers, and arrows fell like rain, but the Unsullied just raised shields until it passed. In the end only six hundred Unsullied remained — but twelve thousand Dothraki lay dead, including Khal Temmo. On the fourth morning the new khal led his men past the gates, each cutting off his braid and throwing it at the feet of the Three Thousand.

paragraphs.context: He could feel the high stone calling him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran, in Summer's skin, runs as a wolf and feels like a prince.
paragraphs.simple: He could feel the high rock calling him. Up he went, running easily at first, then faster. Birds burst from branches as he raced by. He heard the wind in the leaves, squirrels chattering, even a pinecone falling. The smells were a song around him, filling the good green world.

paragraphs.context: Long they fought, rolling together over roots and stones and fallen leaves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Summer fights the old wolf and wins; the old wolf submits.
paragraphs.simple: Long they fought, rolling over roots and stones and the deer's entrails, tearing with tooth and claw, breaking apart, circling, and lunging again. The prince was larger and stronger, but his cousin had a pack. The female circled closely and got between them whenever her mate was bloodied. Others darted in to snap at legs. One angered him so much he whirled and tore out its throat. After that the others kept away. At last the old wolf lay down weary and rolled over, showing throat and belly. It was submission.

paragraphs.context: Remember yourself, or the wolf will consume you.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jojen warns Bran not to lose himself in the wolf.
paragraphs.simple: 'Remember that, Bran. Remember yourself, or the wolf will consume you. When you join, it is not enough to run and hunt and howl in Summer's skin.' It was enough for Bran — he liked Summer's skin better than his own. What good is being a skinchanger if you cannot wear the skin you like?

paragraphs.context: The greenseers were more than that. They were wargs as well, as you are
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jojen explains what greenseers were.
paragraphs.simple: 'No,' said Jojen, 'only a boy who dreams. The greenseers were more than that. They were wargs too, like you, and the greatest could wear the skins of any beast that flies or swims or crawls, and could look through the eyes of the weirwoods, and see the truth beneath the world.'

paragraphs.context: She has broken him, as a man breaks a horse.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos believes Melisandre has broken Stannis and plans to kill her.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre would be waiting on Dragonstone in all her beauty and power, with her god and shadows and his king. She had always seemed loyal to Stannis — until now. She has broken him, as a man breaks a horse. She would ride him to power if she could, and for that she gave Davos's sons to the fire. 'I will cut the living heart from her breast and see how it burns.'

paragraphs.context: Since the battle, he sees no one, but broods in his Stone Drum.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Salladhor describes Stannis's broken little kingdom.
paragraphs.simple: Since the battle, Stannis sees no one but broods in his tower. Queen Selyse holds court with her uncle Lord Alester, who calls himself Hand. It is a little kingdom, poor and rocky. There is no gold to pay Salladhor what he is owed, and only the knights they rescued at the end, and no ships but Salladhor's few.

paragraphs.context: There are shafts, they say, and secret stairs down into the mountain's heart
paragraphs.mainIdea: Salladhor tells of the hungry fires inside the mountain.
paragraphs.simple: The guards keep everyone away, even the queen and little princess. Servants bring food no one eats. Men whisper of hungry fires inside the mountain, and how Stannis and the red woman go down together to watch the flames. There are shafts and secret stairs into the mountain's heart, into hot places where only she can walk unburned.

paragraphs.context: To make an end of Melisandre of Asshai and all her works.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos believes the sea spared him so he can kill Melisandre.
paragraphs.simple: 'And this is why,' said Davos. 'To do this thing. To make an end of Melisandre of Asshai and all her works. Why else would the sea have spit me out? No sensible captain would take his ship through the spears of the merling king. Shayala's Dance should never have come near me.'

paragraphs.context: This is the Inn of the Kneeling Man, my lady.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cleos explains the inn stands where the last King in the North yielded to Aegon.
paragraphs.simple: 'This is the Inn of the Kneeling Man, my lady. It stands upon the very spot where the last King in the North knelt before Aegon the Conqueror to offer his submission.' Jaime added: Torrhen Stark brought his army south after the Field of Fire, but when he saw Aegon's dragon and the size of his host, he chose wisdom and bent his frozen knees.

paragraphs.context: By morning Casterly Rock seemed a small price to pay to be near her always.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime recalls how Cersei talked him into joining the Kingsguard.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei told Jaime their father meant to marry him to Lysa Tully — but if Jaime took the white cloak, he could stay near Cersei always. Jaime objected that their father would never consent. Cersei said the king would not ask him, and once done, Father could not openly object. 'Is it a rock you want? Or me?' That night they met secretly at an inn. By morning, Casterly Rock seemed a small price to pay to be near her always.

paragraphs.context: Jaime's investiture freed him from Lysa Tully. Elsewise, nothing went as planned.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime's plan backfired; his father quit and took Cersei away.
paragraphs.simple: Joining the Kingsguard freed Jaime from Lysa Tully, but nothing else went as planned. His father was furious. He could not object openly, but he resigned as Hand on a thin excuse and went back to Casterly Rock, taking Cersei with him. Instead of being together, Cersei and Jaime just changed places. Jaime was left alone at court, guarding a mad king.

paragraphs.context: A single slash across his throat was all it took to end it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime remembers killing Aerys.
paragraphs.simple: When Aerys saw the blood on Jaime's blade, he demanded to know if it was Tywin's. 'I want him dead, the traitor. I want his head, or you'll burn with all the rest.' 'Rossart's,' Jaime answered. Aerys's eyes grew huge. He lost control of his bowels, turned, and ran for the Iron Throne. Jaime dragged the last dragonking off the steps, squealing like a pig. A single slash across the throat was all it took.

paragraphs.context: So my father decided to nip the rose before it bloomed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys explains why Tywin restored Pycelle: to block a Tyrell Grand Maester.
paragraphs.simple: The Citadel wanted to choose its own Grand Maester and was about to send Maester Gormon, a Tyrell. When Varys told Lord Tywin, he acted at once and restored Pycelle instead. Tyrion laughed: 'So my father decided to nip the rose before it bloomed. Pycelle is a toad. But better a Lannister toad than a Tyrell toad, no?'

paragraphs.context: how could I let this happen again, after Tysha?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion knows he must send Shae away but cannot make himself do it.
paragraphs.simple: For a time Shae said nothing. Tyrion met a wall of cold, polite silence. 'How could I let this happen again, after Tysha? Am I as great a fool as my father thinks?' Gladly he would have promised what she wanted and walked her to his own bedchamber. Had the choice been his, she could have sat beside him at the wedding feast. But he could not watch her hang.

paragraphs.context: Under the beard and the tangled hair was the face
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya recognizes Harwin, her father's man.
paragraphs.simple: Arya whispered 'Harwin?' It was him! Under the beard and tangled hair was Hullen's son, who used to lead her pony and ride at quintain with Jon and Robb. He was thinner and harder, and had never worn a beard at Winterfell, but it was him — her father's man.

paragraphs.context: He has bagged me neat as a hare in a snare.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn realizes Robb has married Jeyne Westerling.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn realized Robb had married Jeyne. Her first thought was 'No, you are only a child.' Her second was 'You have pledged another.' Her third was 'What have you done?' Robb had trapped her — she had already forgiven him. She had no choice but to welcome Jeyne.

paragraphs.context: I've made a botch of everything but the battles, haven't I?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb confesses his failures to Catelyn.
paragraphs.simple: Robb said he had made a mess of everything except the battles. He thought battles would be hard, but if he had kept Theon as hostage, he would still rule the north, and Bran and Rickon would be alive. Catelyn said perhaps, or perhaps not — Balon might still have gone to war.

paragraphs.context: We planned to run Lord Tywin a merry chase up and down the coast
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brynden explains the original plan to trap Tywin in the west.
paragraphs.simple: They were all on horses, while the Lannisters were mostly on foot. They planned to lead Tywin on a chase up and down the coast, then slip behind him to a strong position across the gold road. If Tywin attacked there, he would pay dearly. If not, he would be trapped in the west, far from where he needed to be, while they lived off his land.

paragraphs.context: In Old Nan's stories, giants were outsized men who lived in colossal castles
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon sees real giants, very different from stories.
paragraphs.simple: In Old Nan's stories, giants were big men in castles with huge swords. These were different — more like bears, covered in hair. They were ten to fourteen feet tall, with long arms, short thick legs, no necks, and ugly faces. They rode mammoths and carried clubs, not swords.

paragraphs.context: Mance had spent years assembling this vast plodding host
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mance united the wildling clans into one army.
paragraphs.simple: Mance spent years building this huge slow army, talking to clan mothers and leaders, winning villages with words, songs, or swords, making peace between enemies, hammering a hundred daggers into one great spear aimed at the Seven Kingdoms. He had no crown, but Jon saw he was a king in more than name.

paragraphs.context: But when the dead walk, walls and stakes and swords mean nothing.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mance says only the dead matter, not walls.
paragraphs.simple: Mance said if he had stormed the hill, he would have lost five men for every crow and counted himself lucky. But when the dead walk, walls and weapons mean nothing. No one knows that better than him. He ordered patrols doubled and torches ready.

paragraphs.context: I tell you, these Tyrells are only Lannisters with flowers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dontos warns Sansa the Tyrells want her claim, not her.
paragraphs.simple: Dontos grabbed Sansa's arm and said she cannot marry Willas. The Tyrells are just Lannisters with flowers. She must forget this folly and go ahead with their escape plan on Joffrey's wedding night. Sansa refused — she no longer needs to escape.

paragraphs.context: It's your claim they mean to wed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa realizes she is heir to Winterfell.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa had not forgotten Dontos's words. 'It's your claim they mean to wed.' She grew up with three brothers and never thought to have a claim, but with Bran and Rickon dead... It doesn't matter, there's still Robb. But Willas will have Highgarden — what would he want with Winterfell?

paragraphs.context: That turned the whole world on its head.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Harwin explains how Beric's men became outlaws.
paragraphs.simple: Robert and Ned were dead, and Joffrey was king. That turned the world upside down. They had been sent by the King's Hand to fight outlaws, but now they were the outlaws, and Tywin was Hand. Some wanted to yield, but Beric refused. They were still king's men, fighting for the king's people. For every man they lost, two joined them.

paragraphs.context: I don't care if you're so scared you foul your breeches
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont orders Sam to send the ravens.
paragraphs.simple: Mormont told Sam: 'You're no fighter. If we're attacked, don't get in the way. Send a message. Write it yourself, send one bird to Castle Black and one to the Shadow Tower. I don't care if you're scared, you get those birds off, or I'll hunt you through all seven hells.'

paragraphs.context: Wights over the ringwall. Fighting inside the camp.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam writes messages as the Fist falls.
paragraphs.simple: Sam wrote note after note as the battle turned. Dead wildlings, a giant or bear, all around. Wights over the wall, fighting in the camp. Mormont meeting them with fire. We've won. We're winning. We're holding our own. We're cutting our way free. We're trapped. Lost. The battle's lost. We're all lost.

paragraphs.context: The Other slid gracefully from the saddle to stand upon the snow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: An Other appears and kills Small Paul.
paragraphs.simple: A rider pale as ice sat on a dead horse. The Other slid from the saddle. It was sword-slim and milky white, its armor rippling. Small Paul charged with his axe, but the Other's crystal sword slipped through his mail and out his back. Paul fell, tearing the sword from the Other's grip.

paragraphs.context: King Balon has strangler's fingers round the Neck.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin explains why they won't ally with Balon.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin said Balon has the Neck in his grip. Robb's heirs are dead, Winterfell fallen, ironmen hold Moat Cailin and the Stony Shore. Balon's ships threaten the west. But Greyjoy demands half the kingdom for an alliance — why pay for what he's already doing for free? Better to do nothing and wait for a better option.

paragraphs.context: she will be wed to some Manderly or Umber
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin says Sansa must marry a Lannister.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin said Sansa's happiness is not the point. The key to the north is Sansa Stark. If sent to Riverrun, her mother will marry her to a Blackwood or Mallister. If sent north, she'll wed a Manderly or Umber. She is dangerous at court too. She must marry a Lannister, and soon. Whoever weds her can claim Winterfell.

paragraphs.context: The Young Wolf has taken Gawen Westerling's eldest daughter to wife.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin reveals Robb broke his Frey oath.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin told Tyrion the news: Robb Stark has married Jeyne Westerling, breaking his sworn word to the Freys. Tyrion was stunned. Kevan explained Jeyne's lowborn grandmother was a priestess called Maegi. Tyrion thought Robb chose the girl's honor over his own.

paragraphs.context: Only blood can pay for blood.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Karstark defends killing the squires.
paragraphs.simple: Karstark said his sons died, cut down by the Kingslayer. These two were of his kind. Only blood can pay for blood. Robb said Tion and Willem didn't kill his sons — how is this vengeance? This was folly and murder. His sons died honorably with swords in hand.

paragraphs.context: why would any man ever want to be king?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb despairs over kingship.
paragraphs.simple: Robb cursed them all in despair. Why would any man want to be king? When they shouted 'King in the North,' he swore to be good, honorable, strong, just, loyal, brave. Now he can't tell friend from enemy. Karstark fought beside him in six battles. His sons died for Robb. Yet now Robb must kill their father.

paragraphs.context: With mine own hand I take your life.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb executes Karstark himself.
paragraphs.simple: Robb lifted the axe. 'Rickard Karstark, Lord of Karhold. Here in sight of gods and men, I judge you guilty of murder and high treason. In my own name I condemn you. With my own hand I take your life.' Karstark said, 'Kill me, and be cursed. You are no king of mine.' The axe fell.

paragraphs.context: The dragons always married their sisters.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime fantasizes about marrying Cersei openly.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thought the Starks and Stannis had done him a kindness by spreading the incest tale — now there's nothing to hide. Why not marry Cersei openly? The Targaryens married sisters for hundreds of years. It would ruin Joffrey's claim, but swords won the throne and swords can keep him there.

paragraphs.context: High, low, overhand, he rained down steel upon her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime duels Brienne, chained.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime attacked with Cleos's sword, wrists chained. Brienne parried. He rained steel — high, low, overhand, left, right — faster and faster. She stumbled on a root but recovered. He pinned her against an oak, chased her through a brook. Somehow he could not reach her, as if she had an iron cage.

paragraphs.context: Sunlight ran silver along the edge of the arakh
paragraphs.mainIdea: Vargo Hoat cuts off Jaime's sword hand.
paragraphs.simple: Vargo Hoat said he must send Tywin a message. They yanked Jaime's arms out. The Dothraki drew a huge curved arakh. Jaime thought they meant to scare him — no sellsword would make him scream. Sunlight ran silver along the blade as it came down. And Jaime screamed.

paragraphs.context: I dreamt I saw a shadow with a burning heart butchering a golden stag
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost of High Heart speaks prophecies.
paragraphs.simple: The tiny old woman told her dreams: a shadow with a burning heart killing a golden stag, a faceless man on a swaying bridge with a drowned crow on his shoulder, a roaring river and a woman who was a fish, dead and drifting with red tears. She asked for gifts to pay for her dreams.

paragraphs.context: That way no one can betray him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Harwin explains why Beric stays hidden.
paragraphs.simple: Harwin said Beric moves a lot and never shares plans, so no one can betray him. Hundreds are sworn to him, but they scatter in small bands to strike in a dozen places at once. If one is caught and tortured, they cannot tell where Beric is.

paragraphs.context: Only one boy in three survives it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Unsullied training is brutal.
paragraphs.simple: They are chosen young for size and speed. Training starts at five, dawn to dusk, until they master sword, shield, and spears. Only one boy in three survives. They say on the day they win their spiked cap, the worst is over — no duty will ever be as hard as training.

paragraphs.context: find some wailing newborn, and kill it before its mother's eyes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Unsullied must kill a baby to earn their cap.
paragraphs.simple: To win his spiked cap, an Unsullied must take a silver mark to the slave market, find a crying newborn, and kill it before its mother's eyes. This ensures no weakness remains. Dany felt faint. 'You take a babe from its mother's arms, kill it as she watches, and pay with a silver coin?'

paragraphs.context: Rhaegar fought valiantly, Rhaegar fought nobly, Rhaegar fought honorably.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jorah says Rhaegar lost because he was honorable.
paragraphs.simple: Jorah said all Dany says is true, but Rhaegar lost on the Trident. He lost the battle, the war, the kingdom, his life. His blood ran downriver with his rubies. Rhaegar fought valiantly, nobly, honorably. And Rhaegar died.

paragraphs.context: Dark wings, dark words, me mother used to say
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Liddle reports the Watch is destroyed.
paragraphs.simple: The Liddle said the Old Bear took the Watch into the haunted forest, and only ravens came back, with hardly a message. 'Dark wings, dark words,' his mother used to say, 'but when the birds fly silent, that's even darker.' It was different when there was a Stark in Winterfell.

paragraphs.context: Teach your squire honor, that shall be ransom enough.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Knight of the Laughing Tree defeats the three knights.
paragraphs.simple: The mystery knight was short, in mismatched armor, with a weirwood shield. He challenged the three knights and defeated them all. When they sought to ransom horse and armor, he said in a booming voice, 'Teach your squires honor, that shall be ransom enough.' Their horses were returned after the squires were punished.

paragraphs.context: The Knight of the Laughing Tree had vanished.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mystery knight disappears; the dragon prince wins.
paragraphs.simple: That night, men swore to unmask the mystery knight, and the king urged challenges, saying the helm hid no friend of his. But next morning only two champions appeared — the Knight of the Laughing Tree had vanished. The king was angry and sent the dragon prince to find him, but only the painted shield was found, abandoned in a tree.

paragraphs.context: There are two, Onion Knight. Not seven, not one, not
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre teaches Davos her two-god religion: only R'hllor the Lord of Light and the Great Other exist, and all men must choose between life and light or death and darkness; the wars of kings mean nothing beside this.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre tells Davos there are only two gods, not seven or a hundred: R'hllor, the Lord of Light, and the Great Other, the Lord of Darkness. The war between them has lasted since time began. Every man must choose a side. It is not really about Baratheon against Lannister or Greyjoy against Stark — it is a choice between life and light, or death and darkness. Then she touches his chest and asks: does your heart burn with the light of R'hllor, or is it black and cold and full of worms?

paragraphs.context: When the red star bleeds and the darkness gathers, Azor
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre says the ancient prophecy points to Stannis: the red comet has come and gone, Dragonstone is the place of smoke and salt, and she has seen Stannis leading the fight against the darkness in her flames — he is Azor Ahai reborn.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre says she has seen the truth in her flames: the fires do not lie. An old prophecy says that when the red star bleeds and darkness gathers, the hero Azor Ahai will be born again amidst smoke and salt to wake dragons out of stone. The bleeding star (the red comet) has already come and gone, and Dragonstone is a place of smoke (its volcano) and salt (the sea). So Stannis must be Azor Ahai reborn, the Lord's chosen warrior of fire.

paragraphs.context: he had learned the names of the twelve houses of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon thinks about how he and Ygritte look at the same stars but see different stories — the King's Crown is her Cradle, the Stallion her Horned Lord — and how the Thief was bright the night she says he stole her.
paragraphs.simple: Jon walks through the pines thinking about the stars. Maester Luwin taught him the stars as a boy, and he and Ygritte share some of them, like the Ice Dragon. But the wildlings give the same stars different names: what southerners call the King's Crown, Ygritte calls the Cradle. Ygritte insists that when the Thief (a red star) is in the Moonmaid, it is a lucky time to steal a woman — like the night he stole her, she says.

paragraphs.context: Gendel's folk were never seen again, but on a still
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ygritte tells Jon the scary tale of Gendel's children: lost in the deep caves, their torches failing one by one until only darkness remained — and on still nights their descendants can still be heard sobbing under the hills.
paragraphs.simple: Ygritte tells an old wildling ghost story. Long ago, Gendel led his people through the caves beneath the Wall, but he took a wrong turn and went deeper and deeper. One by one their torches died until there was only darkness. Gendel's people were never seen again — but on a quiet night, Ygritte says, you can hear their children's children's children sobbing under the hills, still looking for the way back up.

paragraphs.context: To go north, you must journey south. To reach the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Quaithe gives Dany a riddle of opposites: to reach her goals she must take the opposite path — go south to go north, pass beneath the shadow to touch the light.
paragraphs.simple: Quaithe speaks in riddles, each line a paradox: to go north you must first journey south; to reach the west you must go east; to go forward you must go back; to touch the light you must pass beneath the shadow. She is warning Dany that the straight path will not work — Dany must take the opposite road to reach what she wants.

paragraphs.context: When she saw the Usurper's rebel host across the river
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany dreams she is Rhaegar riding to the Trident — but mounted on a dragon, melting the ice-armored rebel host with dragonfire — and wakes thinking: this is how it was meant to be.
paragraphs.simple: That night Dany dreams she is her dead brother Rhaegar, riding to the battle at the Trident. But in the dream she rides a dragon, not a horse. Across the river, Robert's rebel army is armored all in ice — and she bathes them in dragonfire until they melt like dew and the river becomes a flood. Part of her knows it is only a dream, but another part exults: this is how it was meant to be.

paragraphs.context: At first glimpse, Dany thought their skin was striped like
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Plaza of Punishment: rebellious slaves flayed alive — peeled in long curling strips like an apple — and hung on crosses, with flies crawling over the raw red flesh.
paragraphs.simple: Riding into Astapor, Dany sees what looks like striped skin on the slaves hanging along the road. Then she rides closer and sees the truth: the crawling black stripes are flies and maggots, and beneath them is raw red flesh. The rebellious slaves have been peeled alive, in one long curling strip, the way a man might peel an apple. She stops beneath one dying man and asks what he did.

paragraphs.context: For after the feast would come the bedding. The men
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa dreads the bedding — the crude wedding custom where guests carry the bride and groom to bed, stripping them with rude jokes, and shout suggestions through the chamber door.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa eats nothing at her own wedding feast. She wants it to end, yet dreads what comes after: the bedding. The men will carry her up to the wedding bed, undressing her on the way with rude jokes about what awaits her between the sheets, while the women do the same to Tyrion. Only when the two are bundled naked into bed will the guests leave — and even then they will stand outside the door shouting ribald suggestions. As a girl Sansa thought the bedding sounded wicked and exciting; now she feels only dread.

paragraphs.context: abed, when the candles are blown out, I am made
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion pleads his case to Sansa: he is ugly and small, but in the dark he is as good as any man — even the Knight of Flowers — and he is generous, loyal, brave, clever, and kind; he could be good to her.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion stands and begs Sansa not to lie to him. He admits he is malformed, scarred, and small — but abed, when the candles are blown out, he is made no worse than other men. In the dark, he says, he is the Knight of Flowers (the famously handsome Ser Loras). He is generous, loyal to those loyal to him, no craven, cleverer than most, and he can even be kind — kindness is not a Lannister habit, but he has some somewhere. He could be good to her.

paragraphs.context: Lord Connington the Hand took the town with a mighty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Harwin tells Arya the story of the Battle of the Bells: Connington searched Stoney Sept house by house for wounded Robert, but Eddard Stark and Hoster Tully stormed the town, and Robert came out of hiding to kill six men.
paragraphs.simple: Harwin tells Arya how Stoney Sept got its name in the war. The Mad King's Hand, Lord Connington, took the town with a mighty force and searched it house by house for Robert Baratheon, who was wounded and hiding. Before Connington could find him, Lord Eddard and Arya's grandfather Hoster Tully came down on the town and stormed the walls. They fought in the streets and even on the rooftops while the septons rang the bells. Robert came out of hiding when the bells rang and slew six men that day — including Myles Mooton, Prince Rhaegar's squire.

paragraphs.context: The bars allowed so little room that prisoners could neither
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horror of the crow cages at Stoney Sept: prisoners can neither sit nor turn, the dead have had their eyes eaten by crows, and one living man croaks for water through a beard thick with blood and flies.
paragraphs.simple: Arya finds the crow cages. The bars leave so little room that the naked prisoners can neither sit nor turn, exposed to sun, wind, and rain. Three cages hold dead men; carrion crows have eaten out their eyes, yet the empty sockets seem to follow her. A fourth man still lives — his ragged beard is thick with blood and flies, and when he speaks the flies explode around his head. 'Water,' he croaks. 'Please… water…'

paragraphs.context: The patrols stumbled on climbers two or three times a year,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon recalls how wildling climbers usually fail: they must leave their horses behind, steal fresh ones, and then the hue and cry goes up and the Watch hunts them down; Jarl won't make that mistake, but the Magnar might.
paragraphs.simple: Jon watches the wildlings climb and thinks about how rarely raiders succeed. Wildlings have scaled the Wall a hundred times and more. Patrols find climbers two or three times a year, and rangers find the broken corpses of those who fell. Climbers must leave their horses behind, so young raiders steal the first horses they find — then a hue and cry goes up, ravens fly, and the Night's Watch hunts them down and hangs them. Jarl is too experienced for that mistake, Jon thinks, but Styr the Magnar is a ruler, not a raider, and may not know how the game is played.

paragraphs.context: "No wall can keep you safe," his father had told him once,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned's lesson: a wall is only as strong as the men who defend it — four determined defenders with arrows and stones could hold off 120 wildlings.
paragraphs.simple: Jon remembers his father's words as they once walked the walls of Winterfell: no wall can keep you safe; a wall is only as strong as the men who defend it. The wildlings may have a hundred and twenty men, but four good defenders would be enough to see them off, with a few well-placed arrows and perhaps a pail of stones. Jon hopes a patrol will chance by and end the wildlings' climb before it begins.

paragraphs.context: Craven, Jaime thought, as Brienne fought to stifle her moans.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime's identity crisis in two lines: with his sword hand gone, he asks whether that is all he ever was — just a sword hand.
paragraphs.simple: Watching Brienne fight to stifle her moans of pain, Jaime calls himself a craven and asks the question that now haunts him: they took his sword hand — was that all he was? Was he nothing but a sword hand? Without his swordsmanship, he does not know who Jaime Lannister is.

paragraphs.context: That was what he'd done, when the Starks had died before
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime teaches Brienne his old coping trick — 'go away inside' your mind during unbearable pain, as he did when he watched Rickard Stark die in his heated armor and Brandon strangle himself trying to save him.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime tells Brienne to let Vargo Hoat's men do what they will, and 'go away inside' — to retreat into her mind where they cannot reach her. It is what he did long ago, when he stood by and watched Lord Rickard Stark die in his heated armor while his son Brandon strangled himself trying to save him. 'Think of Renly, if you loved him. Think of Tarth, mountains and seas,' Jaime whispers — think of anything but this.

paragraphs.context: But Valyrian steel is stubborn. These old swords remember, it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The armorer explains that Valyrian steel resists re-forging: the old swords 'remember' and will not take the Lannister crimson — the blade drinks the sun out of the red dye, and some folds refuse it entirely.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin's armorer apologizes: he tried to dye the reforged Valyrian steel swords the crimson of House Lannister, using half a hundred spells, but Valyrian steel is stubborn. The old swords remember, it is said, and do not change easily. Each time he brightened the red, the color darkened again, as if the blade were drinking the sun out of it — and some folds in the steel would not take the red at all.

paragraphs.context: There's a pot shop I know in Flea Bottom makes a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion coldly orders Symon Silver Tongue's murder: lure him with a broken arm and new court clothes, take his silver tongue — and make sure the rest of him is never found (implied: cooked in the pot shop's stew).
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion gives Bronn his orders about the blackmailing singer. Give Symon three days, then tell him a harper broke his arm and he must be fitted for new court clothes — he will come willingly. Bronn may keep Symon's silver tongue, but the rest of him should never be found. The pot shop in Flea Bottom that makes a famous stew is the unspoken destination: Symon will end up in the pot.

paragraphs.context: I never said, though. Sometimes I think everyone is just pretending
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grenn's honest philosophy: everyone is only pretending to be brave, and none of them really are — maybe pretending is how you get brave.
paragraphs.simple: Grenn admits he gets as frightened as anyone — only Pyp claims he is too dumb to be frightened. Grenn used to be scared of fighting Jon, who was so quick he fought like he meant to kill. But he never said so. Sometimes, Grenn thinks, everyone is just pretending to be brave, and none of them really are. Maybe pretending is how you get brave — he doesn't know. 'Let them call you Slayer,' he tells Sam. 'Who cares?'

paragraphs.context: The Night's Watch has forgotten its true purpose, Tarly. You don't
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont's key insight: the Wall was built to guard the realms of men against the Others — not against wildlings, who are only men — but the Watch lost sight of the true enemy over thousands of years.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Commander Mormont tells Sam the Watch has forgotten why it exists. You don't build a wall seven hundred feet high to keep wildlings in skins from stealing women — wildlings are only men, when you come right down to it. The Wall was made to guard the realms of men against the true enemy. But over hundreds and thousands of years, the Watch lost sight of him. And now he's here, and they don't know how to fight him.

paragraphs.context: If it had been a foul unpleasant smell he might have
paragraphs.mainIdea: The worst horror for Sam: burning Bannen smells like roast pork, and Sam's mouth waters — which horrifies him so much he runs off to vomit.
paragraphs.simple: Sam watches Bannen's corpse burn and the worst thing is the smell. If it had been foul he could have stood it — but his burning brother smells so much like roast pork that Sam's mouth begins to water. That is so horrible to him that when the raven squawks 'Ended,' he runs behind the hall and throws up in the ditch.

paragraphs.context: Six score of us set out to bring the king's justice
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beric tells how the brotherhood began: 120 men sent to bring the king's justice to Gregor Clegane; 80 are dead, but others took up their fallen swords and they fight on for Robert and the realm.
paragraphs.simple: The scarecrow-like man among the weirwood roots is Beric Dondarrion. He tells Arya that when they left King's Landing they were 120 men — knights, squires, lords, and commoners from Winterfell, Darry, and Blackhaven — bound only by their purpose: to bring the king's justice to the men burning the riverlands (Gregor Clegane's raiders). Their leader was 'a fool in a starry cloak' — Beric himself. More than eighty are dead now, but others have taken up the swords that fell from their hands, and with their help they fight on as best they can, for Robert and the realm.

paragraphs.context: A knight's a sword with a horse. The rest, the vows
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound's famous contempt for knighthood: a knight is just a sword with a horse, and the vows and sacred oils are silk ribbons tied round the sword — he's the same as Beric's men but doesn't lie about it.
paragraphs.simple: The Hound sneers at the brotherhood's talk of knighthood. A knight's a sword with a horse, he says. The rest — the vows, the sacred oils, the lady's favors — are just silk ribbons tied round the sword. The sword may look prettier with ribbons, but it kills you just as dead. He's the same as them, he says — the only difference is he doesn't lie about what he is. So kill him, but don't call him a murderer while they pretend their own shit doesn't stink.

paragraphs.context: If there were gods, why didn't Lord Beric win? She knew
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya's crisis of faith: the guilty Hound has killed good Beric, so where are the gods? — and all her stupid prayers for the Hound to die feel like mockery now.
paragraphs.simple: Beric topples with the Hound's sword still in him, and the dirt drinks his blood. Arya can only think of Mycah and all the stupid prayers she prayed for the Hound to die. If there were gods, why didn't Lord Beric win? She knows the Hound is guilty — of Mycah, of everything — and yet the guilty man lives and the good man dies. Her faith cracks.

paragraphs.context: Then, sudden as hope, they saw the red bloom flower. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hoster Tully's river funeral: the Blackfish's flaming arrow is swallowed by the mist — then suddenly the boat's sails bloom red with fire, glowing pink and orange in the fog.
paragraphs.simple: At Hoster Tully's funeral, his body is sent downriver on a boat, and the Blackfish fires a flaming arrow to light the pyre. The boat vanishes into the mist; the falling arrow is swallowed too — but only for a heartbeat. Then, sudden as hope, they see the red bloom flower: the sails take fire, and the fog glows pink and orange. For a moment Catelyn sees the boat clearly, wreathed in leaping flames.

paragraphs.context: "It is no disgrace to miss your shot," her uncle told her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Blackfish comforts Catelyn (and Edmure): missing the funeral shot is no disgrace — even Hoster himself once missed his own father's shot.
paragraphs.simple: When Edmure fails to light his father's funeral boat with his arrow, the Blackfish tells Catelyn quietly: it is no disgrace to miss your shot. Edmure should hear that too. The day the Blackfish's own father went downriver, Hoster Tully — the very man they bury now — missed his shot as well.

paragraphs.context: "I have won every battle, yet somehow I'm losing the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb's despair: he has won every battle yet is losing the war — Winterfell fallen, father and brothers dead, grandfather dying.
paragraphs.simple: Walking with his mother beneath the trees, Robb mutters the sentence that sums up his whole war: I have won every battle, yet somehow I'm losing the war. The ironmen hold Winterfell and Moat Cailin. His father is dead, and Bran and Rickon, maybe Arya. And now her father Hoster too. He looks up, as if the answer might be written on the sky.

paragraphs.context: My brother had a gift for inspiring loyalty. Even in his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis contrasts himself with Robert: Robert turned defeated enemies into friends with sheer charm, while Stannis feels he inspires only betrayal — even in his own blood and kin.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis broods on the difference between himself and Robert. His brother had a gift for inspiring loyalty, even in his foes. At Summerhall, Robert won three battles in one day, took Lords Grandison and Cafferen prisoner — and then drank, feasted, and hunted with them until they loved him. Cafferen died fighting for Robert; Grandison died of wounds taken on the Trident. 'My brother made them love him,' Stannis says bitterly, 'but it would seem that I inspire only betrayal. Even in mine own blood and kin.'

paragraphs.context: Have you ever seen the Iron Throne? The barbs along the back,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis describes the Iron Throne — barbs, ribbons of twisted steel, jagged sword ends, a seat no man can rest on — and wonders why his brothers wanted it so desperately.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis describes the Iron Throne to Davos: the barbs along the back, the ribbons of twisted steel, the jagged ends of swords and knives all tangled up and melted together. It is not a comfortable seat — Aerys cut himself so often men called him King Scab, and Maegor the Cruel was murdered in that chair. It is not a seat where a man can rest at ease. Stannis wonders why his brothers wanted it so desperately.

paragraphs.context: the ashes were white, rising in the updraft, yet all at once
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis tells Davos of his own vision in the fire: falling ash like snow, sparks circling into a ring of torches, men in black moving through snow, a terrible cold — he would stake his kingdom it was real.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis tells Davos what he saw with his own eyes. After the battle, lost in despair, he gazed into the hearthfire at Melisandre's bidding. The ashes were white, rising in the updraft — yet all at once they seemed to be falling, like snow. The sparks circled into a ring of torches, and through the fire he looked down on a high hill in a forest: the cinders had become men in black behind the torches, with shapes moving through the snow. Despite the fire's heat he felt a cold so terrible he shivered — and the sight was gone. But what he saw was real; he'd stake his kingdom on it.

paragraphs.context: Aerys meant to have the greatest funeral pyre of them all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime's confession: Aerys planned to burn all of King's Landing with hidden wildfire rather than surrender it — hoping the flames would transform him and he would rise reborn as a dragon — which is why Jaime killed him.
paragraphs.simple: In the bathhouse, Jaime tells Brienne what he heard as a Kingsguard. When Robert's victory was certain, Aerys ordered his pyromancers to hide 'the substance' (wildfire) all over King's Landing. 'The traitors want my city,' Aerys told Rossart, 'but I'll give them naught but ashes. Let Robert be king over charred bones and cooked meat.' Aerys meant to have the greatest funeral pyre of them all — and, like Aerion Brightfire before him, believed the fire would transform him and he would rise again, reborn as a dragon. That is why Jaime slew him.

paragraphs.context: You want me to absolve you of blame. To tell my
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime's bargain with Roose Bolton: send me to Cersei and I'll sing sweetly of how gently Bolton treated me, blaming the maiming on Vargo Hoat — any other answer and Bolton hands him back to the Goat.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime understands exactly what Bolton wants: absolution. 'You want me to absolve you of blame — to tell my father that this stump is no work of yours.' The deal: send me to Cersei, and I'll sing as sweet a song as Bolton could want, telling how gently he treated his prisoner. Jaime would write it out himself if he had a hand — how he was maimed by the sellsword Jaime's own father brought to Westeros, and saved by the noble Lord Bolton. Any other answer, Jaime knows, and Bolton gives him back to Vargo Hoat (the Goat).

paragraphs.context: There were three sorts of Dornishmen, the first King Daeron had
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion recalls King Daeron's old classification of Dornishmen: the salty (coastal, most Rhoynish blood), the sandy (desert), and the stony (mountain) — the stony having the least Rhoynish blood.
paragraphs.simple: Riding to meet the Dornish, Tyrion remembers what the first King Daeron observed: there were three sorts of Dornishmen. The salty Dornishmen lived along the coasts, the sandy Dornishmen in the deserts and long river valleys, and the stony Dornishmen made their fastnesses in the passes and heights of the Red Mountains. The salty had the most Rhoynish blood, the stony the least.

paragraphs.context: The boy of sixteen was a man past forty now, and his
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Viper's legend: at sixteen Oberyn was caught abed with Lord Yronwood's paramour, fought a duel to first blood — but Yronwood's wounds festered and killed him, and men whispered the sword was poisoned.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion knows Oberyn Martell only by reputation — and it is fearsome. At sixteen, the prince was found abed with the paramour of old Lord Yronwood, a huge fierce-tempered man. A duel followed, only to first blood out of respect for the prince's youth and birth. Both men took cuts and honor was satisfied — but Oberyn soon recovered while Yronwood's wounds festered and killed him. Afterward men whispered that Oberyn had fought with a poisoned sword, and ever after all called him the Red Viper.

paragraphs.context: After all the wonderful whispers, Lord Tywin's Doom turned out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oberyn's cruel story: Cersei showed off baby Tyrion to the Dornish children, then twisted his tiny cock so hard thinking he had killed their mother — until Jaime made her stop.
paragraphs.simple: Oberyn tells Tyrion what happened when he and Elia saw the newborn 'monster' Cersei had promised them in her letters. Cersei even undid the swaddling clothes for a better look: no tail, no beard, neither teeth nor claws — just a hideous red infant with stunted legs. When Oberyn said he seemed a poor sort of monster, Cersei said, 'He killed my mother,' and twisted the baby's little cock so hard Oberyn thought she would pull it off. Tyrion shrieked — and only when Jaime said 'Leave him be, you're hurting him' did Cersei let go.

paragraphs.context: Here is where Ser Burton Crakehall broke helm and head with
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beric shows Arya his death wounds: a mace that broke helm and head, the manticore's mark at Rushing Falls, the Mountain's dirk through his visor — three deaths at House Clegane's hands alone.
paragraphs.simple: Beric points out where he has died. Here, above his left ear, Ser Burton Crakehall broke helm and head with a mace. Here, the black bruise round his neck, the mark of the manticore who hanged him at Rushing Falls along with the beekeeper and his wife he had tried to save. Here, the raw red pit of his eye, where the Mountain thrust his dirk through his visor. 'That's thrice I have died at the hands of House Clegane,' Beric says with a weary smile. 'You would think that I might have learned…'

paragraphs.context: Can I dwell on what I scarce remember? I held a castle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Each resurrection costs Beric his memories: he cannot find his old castle, recall his betrothed's hair, or name who knighted him — sometimes he thinks he was born in that grove of ash with fire in his mouth.
paragraphs.simple: Beric tells Arya what dying again and again has cost him. Can he dwell on what he scarce remembers? He once held a castle on the Marches and was pledged to marry a woman — but he could not find that castle today nor tell the color of her hair. Who knighted him? What were his favorite foods? It all fades. Sometimes he thinks he was born on the bloody grass in that grove of ash, with the taste of fire in his mouth and a hole in his chest.

paragraphs.context: So when his poor torn chest stopped moving, I gave him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros explains the 'last kiss': a funeral rite — breathing fire into the dead man's mouth — but with Beric the corpse shuddered and opened his eyes; it was R'hllor, not Thoros, who raised him.
paragraphs.simple: Thoros says he has no magic, only prayers. The first time Beric died, his chest was torn open and there was no hope — so when the chest stopped moving, Thoros gave him the last kiss, the funeral rite: he filled his mouth with fire and breathed the flames down Beric's throat to lungs and heart and soul. But never before had he felt a dead man shudder as the fire filled him, nor seen his eyes come open. It was not Thoros who raised him — it was the Lord. R'hllor is not done with him yet.

paragraphs.context: Brandon the Builder gave all the land south of the Wall to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran explains the Gift and the New Gift: Brandon the Builder gave the Watch land south of the Wall for its support, and centuries later Good Queen Alysanne doubled it to fifty leagues.
paragraphs.simple: Bran proudly recites the history Maester Luwin taught him. This is the Gift — the New Gift, and north of that Brandon's Gift. Brandon the Builder gave all the land south of the Wall to the black brothers, to a distance of twenty-five leagues, for their sustenance and support. Thousands of years later, Good Queen Alysanne visited the Wall on her dragon and thought the Watch so brave that she had the Old King double their lands to fifty leagues — that was the New Gift.

paragraphs.context: Maester Luwin had once made Bran learn the names of every one
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost castles: nineteen forts along the Wall, never more than seventeen manned at once — Bran once recited them all for Benjen, east to west and back.
paragraphs.simple: Old Nan called them the ghost castles. Maester Luwin once made Bran learn the names of every one of the forts along the Wall — nineteen in all, though no more than seventeen had ever been manned at any one time. At the feast for King Robert's visit, Bran recited them for his uncle Benjen, east to west and then west to east, and Benjen laughed that Bran knew them better than he did. That was before Bran fell, before he was broken.

paragraphs.context: "Nothing." Bran shook his head. "I don't know." But he did.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran realizes with fright that he just slipped into Hodor's mind — he had been Hodor for half a heartbeat.
paragraphs.simple: Jojen asks Bran what happened, and Bran lies: nothing, he doesn't know. But he does know. He reached for Hodor the way he reaches for Summer the direwolf — and for half a heartbeat, he had been Hodor. The realization scares him: he has just warged a human being without meaning to.

paragraphs.context: "The gods made the earth for all men t' share. Only
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ygritte's famous speech: the gods made the earth for all men to share — only kings came with crowns and steel swords and claimed it all; a thief at least must be brave and clever, while a kneeler only kneels.
paragraphs.simple: Ygritte scorns kings and their property. The gods made the earth for all men to share, she says — only when the kings came with their crowns and steel swords did they claim it was all theirs: my trees, my stream, my wood, my earth, my water, my castle, my daughter. You call us thieves, she tells Jon, but at least a thief has to be brave and clever and quick. A kneeler only has to kneel.

paragraphs.context: They fight with reckless courage, every man out for glory. "I don't
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon argues that discipline beats valor: wildlings fight as glory-seeking individuals, and Mance will fail like every King-beyond-the-Wall before him.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Ygritte the wildlings will lose. Wildlings fight like heroes or demons, but it comes down to the same thing: they fight with reckless courage, every man out for glory. But when it comes to battle, discipline beats valor every time. Mance will fail as all the Kings-beyond-the-Wall have failed before him — and when he does, Ygritte and all the rest will die.

paragraphs.context: He is an old man, Jon told himself. Fifty, maybe even
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon cannot kill the old prisoner: his arguments collapse, Longclaw feels heavy as lead, and the memory of his father's justice — the deserter, the brightness of blood on snow — stops his hand.
paragraphs.simple: Ordered to prove himself by killing an old prisoner, Jon freezes. He is an old man, Jon tells himself — fifty, maybe sixty, who lived a longer life than most; the Thenns will kill him anyway. Longclaw seems heavier than lead in his hand, too heavy to lift. The man's eyes are as big and black as wells. Jon remembers another killing — the deserter on his knees, his head rolling, the brightness of blood on snow, his father's sword, his father's words, his father's face — and cannot do it.

paragraphs.context: It was something he had to do, a task the world had set
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan remembers Rhaegar: a great fighter who took no joy in fighting — he loved his harp better than his lance.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Barristan tells Dany about her brother Rhaegar. His prowess was unquestioned, but he seldom entered the lists. He never loved the song of swords the way Robert did. Fighting was something he had to do, a task the world had set him; he did it well, for he did everything well — but he took no joy in it. Men said he loved his harp much better than his lance.

paragraphs.context: He was born in grief, my queen, and that shadow
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rhaegar was born in grief at Summerhall, and that shadow hung over him all his days — the root of his famous melancholy.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan explains Rhaegar's sadness: he was born in grief, and that shadow hung over him all his days. (Rhaegar was born at Summerhall on the day of the great tragedy there.) The sorrow of his birth never left him — it is why the brilliant, gifted prince was always melancholy.

paragraphs.context: "It is Ghiscari, the old pure tongue. It means 'Mother.'"
paragraphs.mainIdea: The freed slaves of Yunkai hail Dany as 'Mhysa' — mother in Ghiscari; she who will never bear a living child realizes she has thousands of children now.
paragraphs.simple: The freed slaves of Yunkai surround Dany, shouting 'Mhysa! Mhysa!' Missandei explains: it is Ghiscari, the old pure tongue — it means 'Mother.' Others call her Maela, Aelalla, Qathei, Tato, but in whatever tongue it all means the same thing. Dany feels a lightness in her chest. I will never bear a living child, she remembers — yet they are all smiling at her, reaching for her, kneeling before her. They are calling me Mother.

paragraphs.context: "I dreamt a wolf howling in the rain, but no one heard his
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost of High Heart's prophetic dreams: a wolf howling unheard in the rain (Robb), a clangor of drums and the saddest little bells (the Red Wedding), a maid with serpents in her hair slaying a giant in a snow castle (Sansa).
paragraphs.simple: The dwarf woman on the hill speaks her dreams: a wolf howling in the rain, but no one heard his grief; a terrible clangor of drums and horns and pipes and screams, but the saddest sound was the little bells; a maid at a feast with purple serpents in her hair, venom dripping from their fangs — and later that same maid slaying a savage giant in a castle built of snow. Then she turns and smiles right at Arya through the gloom: 'You cannot hide from me, child.'

paragraphs.context: "I see you," she whispered. "I see you, wolf child. Blood child.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost recognizes Arya — 'wolf child, blood child' — and begs the 'dark heart' to leave: she gorged on grief at Summerhall and needs none of Arya's.
paragraphs.simple: The dwarf woman studies Arya with dim red eyes and whispers: I see you, wolf child. Blood child. She thought it was the lord (Beric) who smelled of death — but it is Arya. She begins to sob: 'You are cruel to come to my hill, cruel. I gorged on grief at Summerhall, I need none of yours. Begone from here, dark heart. Begone!'

paragraphs.context: The black fish holds the rivers now. If it's the mother you
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ghost sends Arya toward the Twins — her mother will be there, for there's to be a wedding — then speaks the old gods' poetry of past and future.
paragraphs.simple: The dwarf woman tells Arya: if it's your mother you want, seek her at the Twins — for there's to be a wedding. She cackles that Thoros will see it in his fires. This place belongs to the old gods still, she says; they linger here, shrunken and feeble but not yet dead. 'For the oak recalls the acorn, the acorn dreams the oak, the stump lives in them both.' Then she demands her payment: the song Beric promised her.

paragraphs.context: "Us? This is your place, Brother. This is your darkness."
paragraphs.mainIdea: In Jaime's dream, Cersei tells him the lightless cavern under the Rock is his place — his darkness, where he belongs.
paragraphs.simple: In Jaime's dream under Casterly Rock, he asks Cersei why their father brought them there. 'Us? This is your place, Brother,' she answers. 'This is your darkness.' Her torch is the only light in the cavern — the only light in the world. Then she turns to go, leaving him in the dark that is his.

paragraphs.context: "I left my wife and children in your hands."
paragraphs.mainIdea: The shade of Rhaegar accuses Jaime: he left Elia and his children in Jaime's hands — and Jaime let them die.
paragraphs.simple: In the dream, the dead come to accuse Jaime. Prince Rhaegar burns with a cold light — now white, now red, now dark — and speaks the charge Jaime can never answer: 'I left my wife and children in your hands.' Jaime stood by while the Mountain murdered Elia and her children; the guilt follows him into the dark.

paragraphs.context: He ruled from the Trident to the Neck, thousands of years before
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn remembers Tristifer Mudd the Hammer of Justice: last great river king, winner of 99 battles, dead in his hundredth — his house ruled the riverlands a thousand years before the Andals came.
paragraphs.simple: Passing the tomb, Catelyn remembers the story her father told her. Here lies Tristifer, Fourth of His Name, King of the Rivers and the Hills. He ruled from the Trident to the Neck thousands of years ago, when the First Men's kingdoms were falling before the Andals. They called him the Hammer of Justice; he fought a hundred battles and won nine-and-ninety. He died in his hundredth battle, when seven Andal kings joined against him — and with Tristifer the Fifth died House Mudd, which had ruled the riverlands for a thousand years.

paragraphs.context: The Blackfyre pretenders troubled the Targaryens for five generations, until
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn warns Robb: legitimizing Jon would repeat Aegon IV's disaster — his legitimized bastards bred five generations of Blackfyre wars; a legitimized bastard can never be made a bastard again.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn argues bitterly against naming Jon heir. 'Precedent,' she says: Aegon the Fourth legitimized all his bastards on his deathbed — and how much pain, grief, war, and murder grew from that? The Blackfyre pretenders troubled the Targaryens for five generations, until Barristan the Bold slew the last of them. Robb may trust Jon, but can he trust Jon's sons, or their sons? If you make Jon legitimate, there is no way to turn him bastard again — and any sons Robb has by Jeyne will never be safe.

paragraphs.context: "From the south," said Robb. "But if we can attack from
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb's plan for Moat Cailin: attack from north and west at once, catch the ironmen in the rear while they face his main thrust up the causeway, then split twelve thousand men into three battles.
paragraphs.simple: Robb lays out his plan. The ironmen expect attack from the south, up the causeway — but if Robb can attack from the north and west simultaneously, he will take them in the rear while they are beating off what they think is his main thrust. Once he links up with Bolton and the Freys he will have more than twelve thousand men; he means to divide them into three battles and start up the causeway half a day apart, so Greyjoy scouts see his whole strength rushing headlong at Moat Cailin.

paragraphs.context: "Old gods, hear my prayer. The Seven were my father's gods but
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam's desperate prayer at the weirwood: torn between his father's Seven and the Watch's old gods, hungry and freezing, all he can think to say is 'Gilly has a little son.'
paragraphs.simple: Alone before the weirwood with its carved face and weeping red eyes, Sam sinks clumsily to his knees. 'Old gods, hear my prayer. The Seven were my father's gods, but I said my words to you when I joined the Watch. Help us now. I fear we might be lost. We're hungry too, and so cold. I don't know what gods I believe in now, but… please, if you're there, help us. Gilly has a little son.' That is all he can think to say, as the dusk deepens and the leaves rustle like a thousand blood-red hands.

paragraphs.context: The Father's face is stern and strong, he sits and judges
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam remembers the Song of the Seven — a children's rhyme describing each of the seven gods.
paragraphs.simple: Freezing in the dark, Sam remembers the song his mother sang: the Song of the Seven. 'The Father's face is stern and strong, he sits and judges right from wrong. He weighs our lives, the short and long, and loves the little children.' It is a simple rhyming prayer-song that names each of the Seven gods in turn.

paragraphs.context: Yet even so the wight's grip did not loosen. Sam's last
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam kills the wight Paul with fire: as Paul chokes him, a wisp of smoke rises between Paul's broken teeth and the dead man's face bursts into flame — fire destroys wights.
paragraphs.simple: The dead Paul has Sam by the throat and will not let go, even as Sam's last thoughts turn to his mother and the father he failed. Then, as the longhall spins, Sam sees a wisp of smoke rising from between Paul's broken teeth — the torch Gilly dropped must have caught. The dead man's face bursts into flame, and the hands are gone. Fire kills wights.
