paragraphs.context: Shrieking, flapping, they descended on the wights in angry clouds.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rescue: thousands of ravens pour from the weirwood and fall on the wights, pecking at their blue eyes — Sam and Gilly are saved.
paragraphs.simple: As the wights close in on Gilly, the weirwood itself seems to wake: the starlight stirs, the trees groan, and Sam turns the color of curdled milk. Ravens — hundreds, thousands of them — perch on the bone-white branches. Then, shrieking and flapping, they descend on the wights in angry clouds: they swarm round Chett's face and peck at his blue eyes, cover the Sisterman like flies, pluck gobbets from inside Hake's shattered head. There are so many that Sam cannot see the moon.

paragraphs.context: The rain was falling from a black iron sky, pricking the green
paragraphs.mainIdea: The flooded Trident: a mile-wide torrent under a black iron sky, drowned trees clutching at the air like drowning men, a dead animal floating past, a growling rumble at the edge of hearing.
paragraphs.simple: Arya stares at the flooded Trident. Rain falls from a black iron sky, pricking the green and brown torrent with ten thousand swords. The river must be a mile across. Half-drowned trees poke up through the swirling water, their limbs clutching for the sky like the arms of drowning men; mats of sodden leaves choke the shore, and farther out something pale and swollen — a deer or a dead horse — moves swiftly downstream. There is a sound too, a low rumble at the edge of hearing, like a dog just before he growls.

paragraphs.context: "Stupid blind little wolf bitch." His voice was rough and hard
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound reveals his plan: he's done with the Lannisters — he'll ride Arya to the Twins and ransom her to Robb, and maybe be made a lordling for killing Gregor.
paragraphs.simple: The Hound lays out his plan. He's done with Joffrey, the queen, the Kingsguard, the Lannisters — what's a dog to do with lions? They are at the Trident, not the Blackwater; on the morrow they'll reach the kingsroad and ride straight for the Twins. It is the Hound who will hand Arya to her mother — not the brotherhood. Dondarrion took his gold, so he took Arya: she's worth twice what they stole, maybe more if he sold her to the Lannisters — but he won't. If the Young Wolf has sense, he'll make the Hound a lordling and beg him into his service. Maybe he'll even kill Gregor for Robb.

paragraphs.context: Harma Dogshead was seen at Woodswatch-by-the-Pool, Rattleshirt at Long
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wildling feints all along the Wall — sightings everywhere, gone at the first glimpse of a black cloak; Jon sees that Mance wants the Watch to spread itself thin.
paragraphs.simple: Jon reports the wildling movements: Harma Dogshead seen at Woodswatch-by-the-Pool, Rattleshirt at Long Barrow, the Weeper near Icemark — all along the Wall they are here, there, climbing near Queensgate, hacking at Greyguard's gates, massing against Eastwatch. But one glimpse of a black cloak and they're gone; next day they're somewhere else. Jon sees the game: feints. Mance wants the Watch to spread itself thin.

paragraphs.context: A choosing. With Qhorin Halfhand and Ser Jaremy Rykker both dead and Ben
paragraphs.mainIdea: The leadership dilemma: the only candidates are Cotter Pyke (young, bastard-born, rough, bold to a fault) and Denys Mallister (old, courtly, cautious) — and the two despise each other.
paragraphs.simple: Castle Black must choose a new Lord Commander. With Qhorin Halfhand and Ser Jaremy Rykker dead and Ben Stark missing, who is left? Not Bowen Marsh or the senile Ser Wynton Stout. It will be Cotter Pyke or Ser Denys Mallister: the commanders of Eastwatch and the Shadow Tower — good men but very different. Denys courtly and cautious, as chivalrous as elderly; Pyke younger, bastard-born, rough-tongued, and bold to a fault. Worse, the two men despise each other.

paragraphs.context: Balon Greyjoy has crowned himself again and sent his longships against
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon's grim news: Balon Greyjoy has rebelled again, no king will aid the Watch, and Winterfell is no more.
paragraphs.simple: Maester Aemon gives Jon the news from the south: much and more happened while Jon was away, and little of it good. Balon Greyjoy has crowned himself again and sent his longships against the north. Kings sprout like weeds everywhere and the Watch has sent appeals to all of them, yet none will come — they have more pressing uses for their swords, and the Watch is far off and forgotten. And Winterfell… Jon, be strong… Winterfell is no more.

paragraphs.context: "Robb, listen to me. Once you have eaten of his bread and salt,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn reminds Robb of the guest right: once you eat a man's bread and salt, the laws of hospitality protect you beneath his roof — the rule that will govern everything at the Twins.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn warns Robb before they enter the Twins: once you have eaten of his bread and salt, you have the guest right, and the laws of hospitality protect you beneath his roof. It is the most sacred law of Westeros — a host may not harm a guest who has shared his bread and salt. Catelyn clings to this as their shield against Walder Frey.

paragraphs.context: There was something of the vulture about Lord Walder, and rather
paragraphs.mainIdea: Walder Frey's grotesque introduction: a vulture-weasel of an old man — bald, toothless, loose-skinned, sucking the air like a babe — enthroned between two carved towers.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn meets Lord Walder Frey at last. Gout and brittle bones have taken their toll; they find him propped in his high seat, his massive black-oak chair carved into two towers joined by a bridge, its embrace turning him into a grotesque child. There is something of the vulture about him, and rather more of the weasel: bald spotted head thrust out on a long pink neck, loose skin dangling under his chin, runny clouded eyes, and a toothless mouth constantly sucking the empty air as a babe sucks at his mother's breast.

paragraphs.context: They had a Crakehall look about them, and Lord Walder's third
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn coldly judges the Frey girls as breeding stock: she prefers the big-boned Crakehall girls — wide hips to bear children, big breasts to nurse them, strong arms to carry them.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn sizes up Roslin Frey and finds her small and slight — pretty enough, but of Rosby stock, never robust. She much prefers the frames of some of the older Frey girls in the hall, who have a Crakehall look: Walder's third wife was a Crakehall. Wide hips to bear children, big breasts to nurse them, strong arms to carry them — the Crakehalls have always been a big-boned family, and strong. Catelyn is choosing a broodmare for Edmure.

paragraphs.context: The big bad-tempered courser wore neither armor, barding, nor harness
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound and Arya are disguised as poor farmers, but under the rough clothes the Hound wears armor.
paragraphs.simple: The Hound's horse wears no armor. The Hound himself is dressed in cheap stained farm clothes with a hood hiding his face, looking like a poor farmer. But Arya knows that under the farm clothes he wears boiled leather and oiled chain mail. She looks like a farmer's son.

paragraphs.context: The badges on their jerkins were smaller versions of the sigil
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya studies the knight's heraldry and decides she does not know him, so she will not risk revealing herself.
paragraphs.simple: The riders wear badges showing their master's sign: a black pitchfork on a gold band over a red-brown field. Arya had hoped to show herself to northern men, but she does not know this pitchfork knight or whom he serves, so she stays hidden.

paragraphs.context: Roose Bolton was one of them, though. The Leech Lord
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya is frightened because Roose Bolton — the man she fled from at Harrenhal — is here, and she wonders if he knows she killed his guard.
paragraphs.simple: Roose Bolton, called the Leech Lord, is with Robb's army. Arya escaped from him at Harrenhal and killed one of his guards to get away. She is afraid he will recognize her and tell her mother, or punish her.

paragraphs.context: their walls of wet silk lit up like magic lanterns
paragraphs.mainIdea: The camp is full of bright silk pavilions painted with heraldic signs, mixed with plain dark tents.
paragraphs.simple: The lords' tents are made of bright wet silk that glows like lanterns from the lamps inside — pink, gold, green, striped and patterned, painted with birds, beasts, and stars. Arya spots Lord Smallwood's yellow tent with six acorns.

paragraphs.context: The wedding feast began with a thin leek soup
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wedding food is poor — thin soup, cold turnips, jellied calves' brains — unfit for a king.
paragraphs.simple: The feast starts with thin leek soup, then salad, river fish in almond milk, cold mashed turnips, jellied calves' brains, and tough beef. It is bad food to serve a king, and the calves' brains turn Catelyn's stomach.

paragraphs.context: No harm, the king says? No harm? Petyr fell from his horse
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Walder is furious about Grey Wind attacking his grandsons and gives Robb an order: the wolf or the wedding — not both.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Walder complains that Grey Wind attacked the grandsons he sent to greet Robb. He says Robb may keep his wolf or have his wedding, but not both — under his roof, his rule holds.

paragraphs.context: A sword needs a sheath, heh, and a wedding needs a bedding
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Walder calls for the bedding custom — the guests will carry the bride and groom to bed.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Walder says the wedding is not complete without the bedding: the guests will undress Edmure and Roslin and carry them to bed, as custom demands. A sword needs a sheath, he jokes, and a wedding needs a bedding.

paragraphs.context: Catelyn wondered whether it was the prospect of losing her maidenhead
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn remembers her own wedding bedding and thinks how many men here will soon die in battle.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn remembers her own bedding night — the torn gown, the bawdy jokes. She thinks of the men here tonight and wonders how many will be dead before the year is done. Too many, she fears.

paragraphs.context: What just happened there? Doubt gripped her heart
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn sees Edwyn Frey violently refuse Dacey's touch and begins to feel real fear, though she tries to dismiss it.
paragraphs.simple: Dacey Mormont touches Edwyn Frey's arm and he shoves her away violently, saying he is done dancing. Catelyn feels doubt grip her heart. She tells herself she is imagining dangers, like an old silly woman — but something is wrong.

paragraphs.context: they began to play a very different sort of song
paragraphs.mainIdea: The musicians strike up "The Rains of Castamere," and Catelyn feels chain mail under Edwyn Frey's sleeve — it is a trap.
paragraphs.simple: The players start a dark new song — "The Rains of Castamere." Catelyn catches Edwyn Frey and feels iron rings under his silk sleeve: he wears armor. The Freys came armed to the feast.

paragraphs.context: a quarrel sprouted from his side, just beneath the shoulder
paragraphs.mainIdea: The massacre begins — crossbow bolts fly from the musicians' gallery and Robb is shot down.
paragraphs.simple: A crossbow bolt hits Robb's side, then his leg, and he falls. Half the musicians are holding crossbows, not instruments. Smalljon Umber throws a table over Robb as a shield while bolts thud into the wood, and the Freys fall on Robb's guards with daggers.

paragraphs.context: Enough, I say. You have repaid betrayal with betrayal
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn holds a knife to Jinglebell's throat and begs Walder Frey to let Robb go — a son for a son.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn puts her dagger to the half-wit's throat. "Enough," she says. "You have repaid betrayal with betrayal — let it end. Let my son go and we will take no vengeance. I will trade your boy's life for Robb's: a son for a son."

paragraphs.context: the white tears and the red ones ran together
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dying and mad with grief, Catelyn claws her own face and thinks of her children as everything goes red.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn tears at her own face with her nails until blood runs down. She thinks of her children — Rickon, Bran, Arya, Sansa, Robb — and begs Ned to make the pain stop. Then a hand grabs her hair, and cold steel bites her throat.

paragraphs.context: The one in the middle had collapsed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya watches the feast tents collapse and burn — the wedding has become an attack.
paragraphs.simple: The middle feast tent has collapsed, then flames lick up from it, and the other two collapse too, their heavy oiled cloth falling on the men beneath. Fire arrows streak through the air and the screams grow so loud Arya can hear words through the music.

paragraphs.context: The camp had become a battlefield. No, a butcher's den
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya sees the whole camp has become a slaughter, with the castle firing burning pitch at the tents.
paragraphs.simple: The camp is now a battlefield — no, a butcher's shop. Flames reach halfway up the sky, swords are singing everywhere, and the castle is flinging burning oil or pitch at the tents with a catapult.

paragraphs.context: We're here," she shouted. Her voice sounded thin and scared
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya refuses to believe what is happening and begs the Hound to go back for her mother.
paragraphs.simple: Arya shouts that they are here — Robb is just in the castle, and her mother, and the gate is even open. She came so far and begs to go get her mother, her voice thin and scared like a little girl's.

paragraphs.context: Not for her brother now, not even for her mother
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya runs for her own life as the Hound chases her, and his axe strikes the back of her head.
paragraphs.simple: Arya runs — not for her brother now, not even for her mother, but for herself. She runs faster than ever, as Mycah must have run, with the Hound's bloody longaxe behind her. His axe takes her in the back of the head.

paragraphs.context: He had settled Prince Oberyn and his lords in a cornerfort
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion has housed the Dornish far from the Tyrells because the two groups are already fighting, and Oberyn keeps demanding justice.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion put Prince Oberyn and his lords in a distant corner of the castle, as far from the Tyrells as possible. Already a Tyrell man is dead in a tavern brawl and the old Lady Tyrell insulted Oberyn's lover. Every time Tyrion sees Oberyn, the prince asks when justice will be served.

paragraphs.context: trying to track some golden dragons through the labyrinth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion struggles with Littlefinger's accounts and finds some deals smell dishonest.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion tries to follow the gold through the maze of Littlefinger's ledgers, but the accounts make his head hurt. Littlefinger believed in investing gold, not hoarding it — yet some of these ventures smell worse than week-old fish.

paragraphs.context: Roslin caught a fine fat trout,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The coded message means the Starks are dead — the "trout" is Edmure Tully, the "wolf pelts" Robb and Catelyn.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Walder's message is in code: "Roslin caught a fine fat trout" means Edmure Tully is taken, and "a pair of wolf pelts" means Robb and Catelyn Stark are dead. The seal shows House Frey's twin towers.

paragraphs.context: when your enemies defy you, you must serve them steel and fire
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin teaches Joffrey kingship — crush defiance, show mercy to the kneeling — and a true king never says he is king.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin tells Joffrey: when enemies defy you, give them war; when they kneel, help them back up — or no one will ever kneel to you. And any man who must say "I am the king" is no true king at all.

paragraphs.context: No one was told, save those who had a part to play
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin explains he told no one of the plot except those needed, and warns Tyrion his loose tongue will ruin him.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin says no one was told of the Red Wedding except those with a part to play, and only what they needed to know — that is the only way to keep a secret. He warns Tyrion: "That loose tongue of yours will be your undoing."

paragraphs.context: It was necessary to demonstrate our loyalty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin explains he had Rhaegar's children killed to prove House Lannister's loyalty to Robert.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin says they came late to Robert's cause, so they had to prove loyalty: he laid the children's bodies before the throne so no one could doubt they had forsaken the Targaryens. Even Robert knew the children had to die — yet as a "hero," he could not kill children himself.

paragraphs.context: Explain to me why it is more noble to kill ten thousand men
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin lists the rewards promised for the Red Wedding and argues a dozen dead at dinner beats ten thousand in battle.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin names the price: Riverrun for the Freys, Frey brides for Lannisters, and Roose Bolton made Warden of the North. He asks Tyrion: why is it more noble to kill ten thousand men in battle than a dozen at dinner?

paragraphs.context: They swear Lord Frey had the boy's head hacked off
paragraphs.mainIdea: Salladhor reports the Red Wedding — Robb beheaded, his direwolf's head sewn on, Catelyn thrown in the river.
paragraphs.simple: The smallfolk call it the Red Wedding. They say Lord Frey had Robb's head cut off, sewed his direwolf's head on in its place, and nailed a crown about his ears. His mother was killed too and thrown naked in the river.

paragraphs.context: An ant who hears the words of a king
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre says men are like ants before a god — if she misread the flames, the fault is the reader's, not the book's.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre says: an ant cannot understand a king's words, and all men are ants before god. If she mistook a warning for a prophecy, the fault lies in her as reader, not in the flames as book. But she is certain Stannis must show the realm a sign of power.

paragraphs.context: Nine mages crossed the sea to hatch Aegon the Third's cache of eggs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis lists past failed attempts to hatch dragons to show it cannot be done.
paragraphs.simple: Nine mages tried to hatch dragon eggs, Baelor prayed over his for half a year, Aegon built wooden dragons, Aerion drank wildfire to become a dragon. The mages failed, the prayers went unanswered, the wooden dragons burned, and Aerion died screaming.

paragraphs.context: How many boys dwell in Westeros? How many girls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis says his duty to the realm may demand sacrificing one boy to save thousands.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis asks how many boys, girls, men, and women live in Westeros — the darkness will devour them all. He never asked to be king, yet he must do his duty. Dare he disregard Melisandre? What is one boy's life against a kingdom?

paragraphs.context: A smuggler had best know men as well as tides
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos has quietly gathered supporters — knights who doubt Melisandre — "king's men, not queen's men."
paragraphs.simple: Davos has been seeking out knights and lordlings who still follow the old gods and think Melisandre failed Stannis — men like Ser Gerald Gower and the Bastard of Nightsong. King's men, not queen's men. But he will not boast of them.

paragraphs.context: Ser Ryam Redwyne was the greatest knight of his day
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pylos shows Davos that great knights failed as Hand while a blacksmith's son succeeded — low birth is no bar.
paragraphs.simple: Pylos lists the greatest knight, the holiest septon, the wittiest lord — all failed as Hand of the King. But Septon Barth, a blacksmith's son, gave the realm forty years of peace. Davos's doubts about his low birth are groundless.

paragraphs.context: the straw soldiers had been Maester Aemon's notion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maester Aemon's trick — straw men in black cloaks on every tower to fake a strong defense.
paragraphs.simple: The straw soldiers were Maester Aemon's idea: stuff spare clothes with straw, drape black cloaks on them, and set them standing watch on every tower. The hope was the Thenns would see them from afar and decide Castle Black was too well defended to attack.

paragraphs.context: The Night's Watch is pledged to take no part
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon recalls his uncle's lesson — Castle Black has no walls on purpose, so the Watch can never threaten the realm.
paragraphs.simple: Jon's uncle explained: the Watch takes no part in the realm's quarrels. Past Lords Commander grew ambitious and nearly destroyed the Watch, so the Stark in Winterfell made sure their castles could not be defended — the Watch's only foes are north, and to the north stands the Wall.

paragraphs.context: a crescent-shaped barricade ten feet high made of stores
paragraphs.mainIdea: The defenders built a makeshift wall of supplies to guard the gate and the stair to the Wall.
paragraphs.simple: Castle Black has a wall of sorts at last — a crescent barricade ten feet high made of stores: casks, barrels, crates, logs, and sacks of grain. It guards the two things most worth defending: the gate and the foot of the great wooden stair climbing the Wall.

paragraphs.context: a few of them even looked like soldiers. In a bad light
paragraphs.mainIdea: The armed villagers look like soldiers only in bad light — if you squint.
paragraphs.simple: Every villager able to hold a spear must help defend the barricade. Noye armed them with axes, daggers, swords, and maces, and dressed them in leather and mail. A few even looked like soldiers — in a bad light, if you squint.

paragraphs.context: Maester Aemon had sent a lot of birds… not to one king, but to four
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon sent ravens begging for help to four kings and dozens of northern lords.
paragraphs.simple: Maester Aemon sent birds not to one king but to four: "Wildlings at the gate. The realm in danger." Ravens flew to Oldtown, the Citadel, and half a hundred lords — to the Umbers, Boltons, Karstarks, Mormonts, and more — all begging: come with all your strength.

paragraphs.context: With flames below and flames above, the wildlings had nowhere to go
paragraphs.mainIdea: Trapped between fires on the burning stair, the Thenns die — and the stair collapses with Styr.
paragraphs.simple: Wind and fire did the rest. With flames below and above, the wildlings had nowhere to go: some burned, some leapt and died from the fall. Then the ice cracked and the whole lower stair broke off — the last Jon saw of Styr, the Magnar of Thenn.

paragraphs.context: It was here that Night's King had reigned
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran recalls Old Nan's horror stories tied to the Nightfort — the Night's King, the Rat Cook, the sentinels, Mad Axe.
paragraphs.simple: Bran remembers Old Nan's scariest stories, all set here: where the Night's King reigned, where the Rat Cook served his pie, where the seventy-nine sentinels stand watch, where Mad Axe butchered his brothers in the dark.

paragraphs.context: and they all face north. The seventy-nine sentinels, they're called.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran tells the tale of the seventy-nine deserters sealed alive in the Wall, still standing watch in death.
paragraphs.simple: Seventy-nine deserters fled south, but Lord Ryswell returned them to the Nightfort. The Lord Commander sealed them alive in the ice atop the Wall, facing north — in death their watch goes on forever. Years later Lord Ryswell came to take the black and stand beside his son.

paragraphs.context: the tale of Night's King. He had been the thirteenth man
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran remembers the tale of the Night's King — a fearless commander who gave his soul to a strange woman and ruled with dark magic.
paragraphs.simple: The Night's King was the thirteenth Lord Commander, a warrior who knew no fear. He loved a strange woman with skin cold as ice and gave her his soul, ruled the Nightfort with sorcery for thirteen years, and was overthrown when found sacrificing to the Others. His name was forbidden.

paragraphs.context: But he slew a guest beneath his roof
paragraphs.mainIdea: Old Nan's moral — the gods cursed the Rat Cook not for murder but for killing a guest under his roof.
paragraphs.simple: The Rat Cook served a king his own son baked in a pie. The gods turned him into a giant rat — not for murder, for a man has a right to vengeance, but because he slew a guest beneath his roof, and that the gods cannot forgive.

paragraphs.context: like trying to pull a left boot on your right foot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran forces his way into Hodor's mind — harder than entering Summer — and stands on Hodor's legs.
paragraphs.simple: Entering Hodor is nothing like sliding into Summer. It fits all wrong, like pulling a left boot on the right foot, and Hodor's mind is scared and pushes back. But Bran squirms and shoves, gathers the huge strong legs under him, and rises — he is standing, walking.

paragraphs.context: they had nailed a slave child up on every milepost
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Masters nailed 163 slave children along the road; Dany insists on seeing and counting every one.
paragraphs.simple: The Great Masters nailed a living slave child to every milepost along the coast road, arms outstretched to point the way to Meereen. Dany orders them taken down but insists: "I will see every one, and count them, and look upon their faces. And I will remember." The count stands at 163.

paragraphs.context: Strong Belwas was a slave here in the fighting pits
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany explains why she chose Belwas — a slave beating the highborn hero shames the Masters, and he is expendable.
paragraphs.simple: Dany chose Belwas because he was a slave in Meereen's fighting pits: if the highborn hero falls to him, the Masters are shamed, and if the hero wins it is a poor victory. Also, unlike her captains, Belwas leads no troops and gives no counsel — he is the man she can most easily spare.

paragraphs.context: I see no point of weakness,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jorah reports the walls have no weak point and their own food is almost gone.
paragraphs.simple: Jorah has studied the landward walls and sees no weakness. They might mine under a tower, but what would they eat while digging? Their stores are all but exhausted. Without wood they can build no siege towers, ladders, or rams.

paragraphs.context: We'll starve long before they do, Your Grace
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jorah warns they will starve before the city — no food, bad water, sickness spreading.
paragraphs.simple: Jorah warns they will starve long before Meereen does: no food, no fodder, bad river water, and sickness already in the camps — fever and bloody flux. The city is better supplied and can be resupplied by water.

paragraphs.context: And closed with iron grates, Brown Ben admitted
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brown Ben describes the sewers — grates, darkness, waist-high filth, giant rats and worse.
paragraphs.simple: The sewers empty into the river through iron grates, though some have rusted through. Inside is a long foul climb in pitch dark through a brick maze, filth never lower than waist-high, with the biggest rats you ever saw — and worse things.

paragraphs.context: there has been an informer by your side selling your secrets
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan reveals an informer at Dany's side has sold her secrets to Varys since her wedding.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan says Dany is watched, as Viserys was: Lord Varys reported Viserys's every move for years. And since the day Dany wed Khal Drogo, an informer by her side has been selling her secrets, trading whispers to the Spider for gold and promises.

paragraphs.context: that was as cruel a jape as the crown the Freys had placed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion feels his promise to protect Sansa is a cruel joke — she lost everything while House Lannister thrives.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion swore to protect Sansa, but it is as cruel a joke as the crown the Freys put on Robb's wolf-head. Sansa has lost her home and everyone she loved. "Winter is coming," the Stark words warn — and it has come for them with a vengeance. Yet it is high summer for House Lannister. So why is Tyrion so cold?

paragraphs.context: With those whisperings I must buy my life anew each day
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys explains he must serve Cersei too — his spies are his only protection, and he buys his life daily.
paragraphs.simple: Varys says Tyrion's threat cuts deep. He serves Tyrion loyally but must also serve Cersei when he can — how long would she let him live if he were of no use to her? He has no guards or brothers to protect him, only his little birds' whispers, with which he must buy his life anew each day.

paragraphs.context: They look like two huge castles afloat in the morning sky
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa watches two cloud-castles merge into one — a quiet image before the wedding day.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa opens the shutters and sees clouds like two huge castles in the morning sky, with walls, keeps, and wispy banners. The rising sun turns them rose and gold and crimson, then the wind melts them together until only one castle remains where there were two.

paragraphs.context: they broke their fast on honeycakes baked with blackberries and nuts
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wedding-day breakfast is lavish, with musicians and fools performing.
paragraphs.simple: In the Queen's Ballroom they breakfast on honeycakes, gammon steaks, bacon, fish in breadcrumbs, pears, and fiery Dornish eggs. Musicians stroll among the tables while Ser Dontos gallops on his broomstick horse and Moon Boy sings rude songs.

paragraphs.context: Lord Tywin waited until last to present the king with his own gift
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin's gift is a Valyrian steel longsword; Joffrey names it Widow's Wail and hacks Tyrion's book to pieces.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin gives Joffrey a Valyrian steel longsword with a cherrywood scabbard studded with golden lions. Joffrey names it Widow's Wail, then uses it to chop Tyrion's gift — the rare book Lives of Four Kings — into pieces, to everyone's horror.

paragraphs.context: Send a dog to kill a wolf, he said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion realizes Joffrey sent the catspaw to kill Bran — Jaime and Cersei would not, but Joffrey would.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion remembers Joffrey joking about killing wolves. Jaime would never send another man to kill, and Cersei would never use a traceable knife — but Joffrey found a willing fool among the camp followers. Tyrion guesses it was Joff's idea to wait until Robert left Winterfell.

paragraphs.context: The wind has been at your hair, though
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Olenna fusses with Sansa's hairnet — secretly pocketing a poison jewel — while joking grimly.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Olenna straightens Sansa's hair and hairnet, tugging and fiddling — and jokes that if they start killing men at weddings, people will fear marriage even more. She invites Sansa to visit Highgarden, then pats her hair once more before leaving.

paragraphs.context: The jousters were a pair of dwarfs
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dwarf jousters perform — stag knight vs wolf knight — and everyone laughs except Sansa.
paragraphs.simple: Two dwarf jousters enter, one on a dog and one on a pig, one dressed as a stag knight and the other as a wolf knight. The hall roars with laughter at their slapstick — everyone except Sansa Stark, whose eyes are far away.

paragraphs.context: the sound of a man trying to suck a river through a reed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joffrey chokes — clawing his throat, face darkening — as the hall erupts in panic.
paragraphs.simple: Joffrey claws at his throat, his nails tearing his flesh, a terrible thin sound coming from his throat — then silence, which is worse. The hall erupts: shouting, praying, weeping. Tyrion realizes calmly: he is going to die.

paragraphs.context: One of them was missing. Sansa lifted the net for a closer look
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa finds one black amethyst missing from her hairnet and realizes with terror it was the poison.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa's hair cascades down as she pulls off the silver hairnet. The black amethysts from Asshai glimmer — but one stone is missing, leaving a dark empty socket. A sudden terror fills her: the stone must have fallen out in the throne room.

paragraphs.context: If Tyrion did it, they will think I was part of it as well
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa realizes that if Tyrion killed Joffrey, she will be blamed too — they are one flesh.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa wonders if Tyrion poisoned Joffrey — he hated his nephew and brought him wine. But if Tyrion did it, they will think she was part of it: they are man and wife, one flesh, one heart, one soul, and Joffrey killed her father.

paragraphs.context: dared not look down. She kept her eyes on the face of the cliff
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa climbs down the cliff one terrifying step at a time.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa dares not look down. She keeps her eyes on the cliff, checking each step, fingers slipping on the cold stone. Halfway down her arms tremble and she knows she will fall — but she forces herself on: one more step, and one more step. If she stops, dawn will find her frozen to the cliff.

paragraphs.context: A bag of dragons buys a man's silence for a while
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger explains why he killed Dontos — a seller will sell again; gold buys brief silence, a bolt buys forever.
paragraphs.simple: Littlefinger says Sansa's grief is wasted: Dontos sold her for ten thousand dragons, and when he drank it up he would have sold her again. A bag of gold buys a man's silence for a while, but a well-placed crossbow bolt buys it forever. All Dontos did, he did at Littlefinger's order.

paragraphs.context: Always keep your foes confused. If they are never certain who you are
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger teaches Sansa his rule — keep foes confused with purposeless moves — for the game of thrones.
paragraphs.simple: Littlefinger shrugs off motive: he is a thousand leagues away in the Vale. His rule: always keep your foes confused — if they never know who you are or what you want, they cannot guess your next move. Sometimes the best way is to make moves with no purpose. "Remember that, Sansa, when you come to play the game."

paragraphs.context: The boy lived and died believing Robert Baratheon his sire
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime feels strangely little grief — Joffrey lived and died believing Robert was his father, and Jaime never held him.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime is curiously calm. Men are supposed to tear their hair out when their children die — but Joffrey lived and died believing Robert Baratheon was his father. Jaime saw him born but never held him; Cersei warned it would look bad.

paragraphs.context: Only strength keeps such men in their place
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime tells Brienne great lords must show strength or bannermen turn — as Walder Frey did.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime explains that every great lord has unruly bannermen who envy his place — his father had the Reynes, the Tyrells have the Florents. Only strength keeps such men loyal; the moment they smell weakness, they turn, as Walder Frey turned on the Starks.

paragraphs.context: You are the heir to Casterly Rock
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin orders Jaime to quit the Kingsguard, take the Rock, and marry — Jaime refuses it all.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin tells Jaime his duty is to House Lannister: leave the Kingsguard, take Casterly Rock as heir, take Tommen as ward, and marry — perhaps even Margaery. Jaime shouts "No!" again and again — he is the Lord Commander of the Kingsguard and nothing else. Tywin answers: "You are not my son."

paragraphs.context: Any cat may stare into a fire and see red mice at play
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre explains reading flames is hard — like a book whose letters dance — and mocks easy claims.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre tells Davos fire is a living thing, always moving like a book whose letters dance as you read. It takes years to see shapes in flames, and more years to tell what will be from what may be. When Davos asks how Ser Axell learned so fast, she smiles: any cat may stare into a fire and see red mice at play.

paragraphs.context: a few acres of good land, a hall to grow old in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos reflects he rose too high — all he ever wanted was land, a hall, and a better life for his sons.
paragraphs.simple: Davos thinks he rose too high and too fast, like climbing a mountain where the air is too thin. As a boy he dreamed of riches; grown, he wanted only a few acres, a timbered roof, and a better life for his sons. If he survives this night, he will take Devan and sail home and speak no more of kings.

paragraphs.context: opened up the poor thing with a dagger to see if it were true
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis recalls boy-Joffrey cutting open a pregnant cat — and says his killer served the kingdom well.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis remembers: cooks told young Joffrey a kitchen cat had kittens in her belly, so Joffrey cut her open with a dagger to see if it was true, then showed the kittens to Robert — who hit him so hard Stannis thought he'd killed him. "Dwarf or leech," Stannis says of Joffrey's killer, "this killer served the kingdom well."

paragraphs.context: Is not Edric Storm one of your people
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos defends himself — his oath was to protect Stannis's people, and Edric is one of them.
paragraphs.simple: Davos reminds Stannis of his oath: to give honest counsel, defend the realm, and protect his people. "Is not Edric Storm one of your people? One of those I swore to protect? I kept my oath. How could that be treason?"

paragraphs.context: You are no Stark, he could hear them mutter, in heavy granite voices
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon dreams of Winterfell's crypts, where the stone kings tell him he is no Stark and has no place there.
paragraphs.simple: Jon dreams he is back in Winterfell, limping past the stone kings on their thrones. Their granite eyes follow him and their granite voices mutter: "You are no Stark... There is no place for you here. Go away." He calls for his father, Bran, Rickon, Benjen — no one answers. He begs forgiveness from Ygritte, but finds only a bloodied direwolf.

paragraphs.context: Ghost had shared his cell before the ranging
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon wakes cold and alone — Ghost and Ygritte both gone — and fears Ghost may be dead.
paragraphs.simple: Jon wakes in his own bed, cold even under the furs. Ghost used to share his cell and warm it; in the wild, Ygritte slept beside him. Both gone now. He burned Ygritte himself, as she would have wanted — and where is Ghost? The wolf in his dream was grey, like Bran's wolf. Had the Thenns killed him? If so, Bran was lost to him for good and all.

paragraphs.context: as if he'd dreamt that night
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon's night blurs into a dream of arrows, mammoths, and a broken trebuchet.
paragraphs.simple: The night blurs like a dream: Jon's archers fire at unseen men while wildling arrows fly back. A mammoth dies at their feet; another burns through the woods. Hours of shocks knock a trebuchet's counterweight loose, wrenching the arm sideways. The left trebuchet keeps throwing, but the wildlings learn to shun where its loads land.

paragraphs.context: a wasteland of blackened grass, bubbling pitch, shattered stone, and corpses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dawn reveals a wasteland of corpses — but behind the dead giants waits the whole wildling host.
paragraphs.simple: The rising sun sends pale lances of light across the battleground. In half a night they turned it into a wasteland of blackened grass, bubbling pitch, shattered stone, and corpses. Crows gather on the burned mammoth. Giants lie dead — but behind them, more is coming.

paragraphs.context: Beneath the trees were all the wildlings in the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon sees the entire wildling host arrayed — the night's fight was only a probe.
paragraphs.simple: Beneath the trees wait all the wildlings in the world: raiders, giants, wargs, skinchangers, mountain men, cannibals, cave dwellers — all Mance gathered to break the Wall. Jon realizes the battle with the Magnar was nothing, the night fight less than nothing — only a probe, a dagger in the dark. The real battle is only now beginning.

paragraphs.context: It was a hollow place, an emptiness where her heart had been
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya wakes to a hole inside her — an emptiness where her heart and family were; she believes it will never heal.
paragraphs.simple: Every morning Arya feels a hole inside her — not hunger, but a hollow emptiness where her heart was, where her brothers and parents lived. Her head still hurts, though the lump is going down. But the hole stays the same. "The hole will never feel any better," she tells herself at night.

paragraphs.context: her jaw closed around a pale white arm
paragraphs.mainIdea: In wolf-dream, Arya drags her mother's corpse from the river and begs her to rise.
paragraphs.simple: In her wolf-dream, Arya swims after the scent of death and her jaw closes around a pale white arm — her mother's corpse. She drags it to shore, snarls off her brothers who would feed, and thinks: "Rise. Rise and eat and run with us." But there is only death and blood in her mouth.

paragraphs.context: the Stone Crows, the Milk Snakes, the Sons of the Mist, all of them
paragraphs.mainIdea: The elder warns the high passes are impassable — snow, beasts, and armed clans watch the road.
paragraphs.simple: The village elder warns: frost and snow in the high passes, shadowcats and cave bears — and the clans. The Burned Men, Stone Crows, Milk Snakes, Sons of the Mist have steel now and watch the high road. They'd kill the Hound and make off with Arya. His dream of selling her to Lady Arryn dies there.

paragraphs.context: Will I be allowed to demand trial by battle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion learns his judges will be his father, Lord Tyrell, and the Red Viper — and asks for trial by battle.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion asks who will judge him. Ser Kevan says: his father (the Hand), plus Lord Tyrell and Prince Oberyn. Tyrion is scarcely reassured — Tyrell was Joffrey's goodfather, and the Red Viper is a snake. "Will I be allowed to demand trial by battle?"

paragraphs.context: Bronn would make short work of any of the three brothers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei plans to name Gregor Clegane as champion — Bronn could beat the Kettleblacks, but not the Mountain.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion realizes Cersei checks his moves before he makes them: she means to name Ser Gregor Clegane as her champion. Bronn would make short work of any Kettleblack, but the Mountain That Rides is a kettle of a different color. "I shall need to sleep on this."

paragraphs.context: That boy had wanted to be Ser Arthur Dayne
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime reflects his heroes are all dead — and the boy who wanted to be Arthur Dayne became the Smiling Knight instead.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thinks the world was simpler when he was fifteen, and men were made of finer steel. But all his heroes are in their graves now — Arthur Dayne, the Smiling Knight, the White Bull. "And me, that boy I was… when did he die, I wonder? That boy had wanted to be Ser Arthur Dayne, but someplace along the way he had become the Smiling Knight instead."

paragraphs.context: was the home of your childhood, Sansa, but you are no longer a child
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger reveals the tower is his ancestral home — and tells Sansa Winterfell is gone; she must make her own home.
paragraphs.simple: Littlefinger shows Sansa his ancestral home — a nameless tower. He tells her she is not sailing to Winterfell: it has been taken, burned, and sacked, and all she knew and loved are dead. "Winterfell was the home of your childhood, Sansa, but you are no longer a child. You're a woman grown, and you need to make your own home."

paragraphs.context: So we shall tell Lysa's people that you are my natural daughter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger gives Sansa a new identity — his bastard daughter Alayne.
paragraphs.simple: Littlefinger warns: Varys has informers everywhere, and it is not safe to be a Stark. They will tell Lysa's people Sansa is his natural daughter. Sansa suggests being named after her mother — Catelyn is too obvious, but "Alayne" (after his mother) will serve. "So, who are you?"

paragraphs.context: When he closed his eyes he dreamed of fighting; when he woke he fought
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon cannot remember the last time he slept — he dreams of fighting and wakes to fight.
paragraphs.simple: Jon cannot remember the last time he slept. When he closes his eyes he dreams of fighting; when he wakes he fights. Even in the King's Tower he hears the ceaseless thunk of bronze and flint biting into wood — Mance's men chopping, day and night.

paragraphs.context: The turtle was a hull turned upside down and opened fore and aft
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon studies Mance's "turtle" — an upside-down ship hull on wheels, armored with mammoth hide.
paragraphs.simple: Through the Myrish eye Jon studies the wildlings' "turtle": a rounded top, eight huge wheels, a stout wooden frame — an upside-down ship hull, opened fore and aft, a longhall on wheels. The wildlings skinned a dead mammoth and lashed the raw bloody hide over its roof, one more layer atop sheepskins and pelts.

paragraphs.context: I wish I had enough poison for you all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion confesses only to being a dwarf — then wishes he had poisoned them all, and demands trial by battle.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion confesses: "I am guilty of being a dwarf, I confess it." He has been on trial for being a dwarf his entire life. "I did not do it. Yet now I wish I had. I wish I had enough poison for you all." He will get no justice here — so he appeals to the gods and demands trial by battle.

paragraphs.context: each man pointing at the next
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany had 163 masters nailed to posts — and now doubts whether it was just.
paragraphs.simple: Dany had 163 masters nailed to wooden posts around the plaza, each man pointing at the next. Her anger was fierce and hot when she gave the command; she felt like an avenging dragon. But later, passing the dying men, hearing their moans and smelling their blood — "It was just. It was. I did it for the children."

paragraphs.context: He was a butcher in Grazdan's kitchen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany learns the "Great" King Cleon of Astapor was once a kitchen butcher.
paragraphs.simple: Missandei whispers: King Cleon the Great was once a butcher in Grazdan's kitchen — said to slaughter a pig faster than any man in Astapor. "I have given Astapor a butcher king," Dany thinks, feeling ill — but she must not let the envoy see it.

paragraphs.context: I had the honor to meet you at Winterfell when King Robert came
paragraphs.mainIdea: A girl claiming to be Arya Stark is sent north to marry Ramsay Bolton — Jaime knows she is a fraud.
paragraphs.simple: A skinny hollow-eyed girl in a grey cloak pinned with a wolf's-head clasp says, "I'm Arya Stark." Jaime thinks she looks older than the Arya he knew. She is to wed Ramsay Bolton. "The real Arya Stark was buried in some unmarked grave in Flea Bottom in all likelihood. With her brothers dead, and both parents, who would dare name this one a fraud?"

paragraphs.context: I made a botch of that
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon reflects his name will be shadowed — remembered as turncloak, oathbreaker, murderer.
paragraphs.simple: Jon thinks of what men say of bastards — wanton and treacherous. He meant to prove them wrong, to be as good a son as Robb. "I made a botch of that." Robb became a hero king; if Jon is remembered at all, it will be as a turncloak, an oathbreaker, and a murderer. He is glad Eddard is not alive to see his shame.

paragraphs.context: We're not sending you to talk with Mance Rayder
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slynt and Thorne reveal the mission — Jon is sent not to parley, but to kill Mance.
paragraphs.simple: Slynt and Thorne reveal the truth: "We're not sending you to talk with Mance Rayder. We're sending you to kill him." Jon is not fit to kill a kitten. But with Aemon insisting on his innocence, this was better for them. Qhorin's words: "Our honor means no more than our lives, so long as the realm is safe."

sentences.context: But no sooner had it gone than it came again, louder and longer.
sentences.grammar: 'No sooner... than' means 'as soon as'; the helping verb ('had') comes before the subject.
sentences.simple: As soon as the first horn sound stopped, it started again, louder and longer.

sentences.context: You do not throw away your shield for no good purpose
sentences.grammar: Two quoted speeches are joined in one long sentence; the second speaker answers the first one's argument.
sentences.simple: You should not waste your best defense without a good reason.

sentences.context: As well dress a cow in silk as this one.
sentences.grammar: 'As well do X as Y' is an old form of 'might as well'; the sentence leaves out words ('you might').
sentences.simple: You might as well dress a cow in silk as dress her in silk — it would look just as wrong.

sentences.context: all that occurs to me is to go at them with a sword.
sentences.grammar: 'All that occurs to me is...' means 'the only thing I can think of is...'; the long subject comes first.
sentences.simple: The only idea I have is to attack them with a sword.

sentences.context: the loyalty that many of the folk of Riverrun would still feel
sentences.grammar: A long sentence with a 'that'-clause inside a 'that'-clause; the main point comes at the very end.
sentences.simple: Ser Desmond feared she would use the love the people of Riverrun still felt for their lord's daughter to cause more trouble.

sentences.context: slitting his throat when he knelt to pick up the worn iron coin
sentences.grammar: A long list of crimes in one sentence; 'slitting his throat' describes how she killed him, and the 'that'-clause tells which coin it was.
sentences.simple: She killed a guard at the back gate by cutting his throat when he bent down to pick up the coin Jaqen had given her.

sentences.context: hoping against hope that at this hour there would be no one to see and smile
sentences.grammar: 'Hoping against hope' = hoping with almost no chance; three 'no one' clauses pile up what he fears.
sentences.simple: He hoped desperately that no one would see him being carried like a baby and laugh or spread the story.

sentences.context: so she might loose her shadow child.
sentences.grammar: 'So she might...' = 'so that she could...'; 'might' here shows purpose, an old-fashioned use.
sentences.simple: You rowed her into Storm's End at night so that she could release her shadow baby.

sentences.context: Guest right or no, Jon Snow knew he walked on rotten ice here.
sentences.grammar: 'Guest right or no' = 'whether or not there is guest right'; 'noun + or no' means 'whether or not'.
sentences.simple: Whether or not guest right protected him, Jon knew he was in great danger.

sentences.context: or so the songs would have us believe
sentences.grammar: 'Or so X would have us believe' = 'according to X'; it signals that this may be just a story.
sentences.simple: ...if the songs are telling the truth.

sentences.context: however strong or fast or skilled a knight may be
sentences.grammar: 'However + adjective + subject + may be' = 'no matter how...'; a concession clause.
sentences.simple: No matter how strong, fast, or skilled a knight is.

sentences.context: Up he went, loping easy at first, then faster and higher
sentences.grammar: The direction word ('Up') comes before the subject ('he') for emphasis — an inverted word order.
sentences.simple: He went up, running easily at first, then faster and higher.

sentences.context: Gladly would he have given her the promise she wanted
sentences.grammar: The adverb ('Gladly') comes first for emphasis, so the helping verb ('would') comes before the subject ('he') — an inverted word order.
sentences.simple: He would gladly have promised her what she wanted and walked her to his own bedroom.

sentences.context: Were my sons no more than a lesson for a king, then?
sentences.grammar: A rhetorical question — Davos asks but expects no answer; the question expresses grief and anger at the waste of his sons' lives.
sentences.simple: Davos asks himself in bitter anger: did my four sons die only so that Stannis could learn a lesson? He cannot bear the thought that their deaths meant so little.

sentences.context: which made Jarl a sort of good brother once removed to
sentences.grammar: 'Good brother' is an old word for brother-in-law; 'once removed' means one step away in the chain of marriages.
sentences.simple: Jarl married Val. Val's sister Dalla is Mance Rayder's queen, which makes Mance Val's 'good brother' (brother-in-law) — and Jarl is one step further away in the marriage chain.

sentences.context: the smell of pine needles, tugging at his faded blacks.
sentences.grammar: 'Blacks' is used as a noun meaning his black clothes; 'faded' means the color has worn pale. The wind 'sighing' and 'tugging' is personification — it acts like a living thing.
sentences.simple: The wind pulled at Jon's old black Night's Watch clothes, worn pale with age.

sentences.context: he might prove just as poor a warg as a sworn brother
sentences.grammar: A compressed double comparison: 'as poor a warg as a sworn brother and a spy' means 'as poor at being a warg as he has been at being a sworn brother and a spy.'
sentences.simple: Jon fears he will turn out to be as bad at warging (entering an animal's mind) as he has been at being a Night's Watch brother and at spying on the wildlings.

sentences.context: Westeros is being wealthy, yes, but you are not being queen now.
sentences.grammar: Broken Common Tongue: the Astapori wrongly adds '-ing' to 'be' ('is being wealthy'). Strip the extra 'being' to get the plain meaning: 'Westeros is wealthy … you are not queen.'
sentences.simple: The slave means: 'Westeros is wealthy, but you are not its queen.' Dany may be the mother of dragons, but she has no kingdom yet.

sentences.context: My father did. One of the Aegons did too. The third one,
sentences.grammar: 'The third one, or the fourth' is Joffrey correcting himself mid-thought; the broken, careless sentence shows he does not care enough to remember which king it was.
sentences.simple: Joffrey says kings may keep whores — his father Robert did, and one of the Targaryen kings named Aegon did too. He cannot remember which Aegon, the third or the fourth — showing how carelessly he treats even his own family's history.

sentences.context: "Her and this other wench, the one who slew Renly.
sentences.grammar: 'Her' is rough dialectal speech for 'she'; 'come the morn' means 'when morning came.' Tansy's claim is false gossip — Catelyn freed Jaime to trade him for her daughters, not for love.
sentences.simple: Tansy gossips that Catelyn spent the night in Jaime's cell with him and Brienne (the woman who killed Renly), and freed him in the morning 'for love' — a false, dirty rumor.

sentences.context: that the Wall was a sword east of Castle Black, but a snake
sentences.grammar: A metaphor about the Wall's shape: straight as a sword in the east, winding as a snake in the west.
sentences.simple: East of Castle Black the Wall runs straight as a sword; west of it the Wall twists and turns like a snake.

sentences.context: That is true for them as well. It was all in where you stood.
sentences.grammar: 'It was all in where you stood' = it all depended on your point of view; Jon contrasts how southerners and wildlings see the same Wall.
sentences.simple: In the Seven Kingdoms they say the Wall marks the end of the world — and that is true for the wildlings too. Whether the Wall is 'the end of the world' depends on which side you stand on.

sentences.context: "Stop telling me what do, wench. I'll die if it pleases me."
sentences.grammar: Colloquial speech drops the 'to': 'what do' = 'what to do.' 'If it pleases me' is a formal-sounding way to say 'if I want to.'
sentences.simple: Jaime snaps at Brienne: stop telling me what to do. If I want to die, I will.

sentences.context: The wench has built a fortress inside herself.
sentences.grammar: A metaphor: Brienne protects her inner self the way a fortress protects a city; Jaime admires how she endures by 'going away inside.'
sentences.simple: Brienne has built a castle inside her mind — she retreats there during pain and suffering, where no one can hurt her.

sentences.context: "You mistake me. My father is the King's Hand. I am no longer
sentences.grammar: Wordplay: the King's Hand rules through his council, sometimes called his fingers; Tyrion, dismissed from the council, is 'no longer even a finger.'
sentences.simple: Tyrion makes a bitter joke: his father is the King's Hand, but Tyrion himself is no longer even a finger — he has lost his seat on the small council, the Hand's 'fingers.'

sentences.context: Others might like my tune better. The queen, perhaps. Or your lord father.
sentences.grammar: Veiled blackmail: Symon never states the threat openly — 'others might like my tune better' means 'I will take my song to your enemies unless you pay.'
sentences.simple: Symon threatens Tyrion indirectly: if Tyrion won't pay for his song about Shae, perhaps the queen or Lord Tywin would like to hear it better — i.e., pay me or I'll sing it to Cersei or your father.

sentences.context: is it the cold that brings the wights, or the wights
sentences.grammar: A balanced riddle built on a mirror structure — 'is it A that brings B, or B that brings A?' — asking which causes which.
sentences.simple: Sam asks a cause-and-effect riddle: does the cold bring the wights, or do the wights bring the cold? Neither he nor Grenn knows which causes which.

sentences.context: "The boy's brothers," said the old woman on the left. "Craster's sons.
sentences.grammar: Two short fragments carry the horror by implication: the old woman never says what happens to Craster's sons — the reader must infer they are sacrificed to the Others.
sentences.simple: Gilly's baby is a boy — and like all of Craster's sons, he will be given to the Others in the woods. 'They' are coming for him; the old woman names what everyone fears.

sentences.context: "Robert is the king of the worms now.
sentences.grammar: Bitter sarcasm: 'king of the worms' means a dead king, food for worms; the Hound mocks men who claim to fight for a dead man's cause.
sentences.simple: The Hound sneers: Robert is dead — he is food for worms now. He mocks the brotherhood for hiding underground 'to keep his court' when their king is a corpse.

sentences.context: Even Jeyne Poole was not so blind as to think this man was fair.
sentences.grammar: 'Not so blind as to think X' = not foolish enough to believe X; 'fair' here means handsome, and Beric's wounds have destroyed his looks.
sentences.simple: Beric is now so disfigured that even Jeyne Poole — who is not foolish — could not think him handsome.

sentences.context: Bran and Rickon will be waiting for him, Catelyn thought sadly,
sentences.grammar: 'As once I used to wait' reaches back to Catelyn's girlhood, when she waited for Hoster to return; now the waiting is reversed — her dead sons wait for him in death.
sentences.simple: Catelyn thinks: Bran and Rickon (believed dead) will be waiting for their grandfather in death — as she herself once waited for her father to come home. The sentence joins her childhood waiting with her grief.

sentences.context: must leave no single sprig of House Stark alive to dispute their right.
sentences.grammar: 'Sprig' = a small shoot or twig; here it is a metaphor for the last surviving Stark. 'Dispute their right' = challenge their claim to rule.
sentences.simple: To hold the north, the Greyjoys must kill every last Stark — 'sprig' (a small twig) means the last surviving branch of House Stark — so no one can challenge their claim.

sentences.context: daughter to one king and mother to two more, yet she died
sentences.grammar: Compressed history in one clause: 'daughter to one king and mother to two more' packs Rhaenyra's whole royal standing into eight words before the fall — 'yet she died a traitor's death.'
sentences.simple: Rhaenyra Targaryen was the daughter of one king and the mother of two more kings — yet she was executed as a traitor for trying to take her brother's crown. Stannis uses her to show that treason is always punished, whatever your blood.

sentences.context: "By what right does the wolf judge the lion? By what right?"
sentences.grammar: A rhetorical question using house sigils as names: the wolf = Eddard Stark, the lion = Jaime Lannister. 'By what right' challenges the judge's authority, not the verdict.
sentences.simple: Jaime demands: what gave Ned Stark (the wolf) the authority to judge him (the lion)? Ned only had to look at Jaime to find him guilty, without hearing his reasons.

sentences.context: won the war on the battlefield and lost it in a bedchamber, poor fool.
sentences.grammar: A balanced antithesis: 'won the war on the battlefield / lost it in a bedchamber' — the parallel structure contrasts Robb's military victories with the single private act that undid them.
sentences.simple: Robb won every battle but lost the war in a bedchamber — by breaking his marriage promise to the Freys and wedding Jeyne Westerling instead. Jaime pities the 'poor fool.'

sentences.context: "Why, if the gods were cruel, they would have made me my mother's firstborn,
sentences.grammar: A contrary-to-fact condition ('if the gods were cruel, they would have…') expressing relief: Oberyn thanks the gods they did NOT make him the heir, because his violent nature would make him a bad ruler.
sentences.simple: Oberyn is glad he is NOT the ruling prince of Dorne: he is too bloodthirsty to rule. If the gods were cruel, they would have made bloodthirsty him the firstborn heir, and the patient, prudent Doran the third son.

sentences.context: "Even brave men blind themselves sometimes, when they are afraid to see,"
sentences.grammar: 'Blind themselves' is reflexive and metaphorical: not making oneself literally blind, but refusing to see an unpleasant truth out of fear.
sentences.simple: Beric means that Lem is refusing to see the truth: Thoros did not 'heal' Beric — Beric died six times, and each return costs him more of his memories. Lem blinds himself because he is afraid to see it.

sentences.context: "By night all cloaks are black, Your Grace.
sentences.grammar: A proverb-like general truth ('by night' = at night, all cloaks look black) used as a gentle evasion: Jojen avoids answering directly whether the men were Night's Watch.
sentences.simple: Jojen says: at night you cannot tell colors apart — so he could not tell whether the men they saw wore black (Night's Watch) cloaks. It is a proverb-like way of saying darkness hides the truth.

sentences.context: and he would suddenly be reminded of the wall between their worlds.
sentences.grammar: The lowercase 'wall' is deliberate: it echoes the great Wall of ice but means the invisible cultural divide between Jon's wildling life and his Night's Watch loyalty.
sentences.simple: Jon would suddenly remember the invisible divide between his two lives: wildling and Night's Watch. The 'wall' here is lowercase on purpose — it is not the Wall of ice, but the barrier between their worlds.

sentences.context: And I shall be betrayed twice more, once for gold and once for love.
sentences.grammar: A callback to the earlier prophecy; the parallel 'once for gold and once for love' echoes the formal, doom-laden language of the Undying's riddle.
sentences.simple: This recalls the prophecy Dany heard in the House of the Undying: she would be betrayed three times — once for blood, once for gold, and once for love. Two betrayals are still to come.

sentences.context: the oak recalls the acorn, the acorn dreams the oak, the stump lives
sentences.grammar: Three parallel clauses with mirrored word order (oak/acorn, acorn/oak) create a chant-like rhythm; 'the stump lives in them both' unites past and future in the weirwood.
sentences.simple: The ghost's poetry about the old gods: the grown oak remembers being an acorn (the past), the acorn dreams of becoming the oak (the future), and the weirwood stump holds both — the old gods see past and future at once.

sentences.context: I won a prize once, riding at rings."
sentences.grammar: 'Riding at rings' is a gerund phrase naming a sport: 'to ride at' something means to charge toward it on horseback — here, tilting at rings as a target.
sentences.simple: The old squire (the ghost's companion) once won a prize in 'riding at rings' — a tourney game where riders on horseback try to spear small hanging rings with their lances.

sentences.context: but Jaime only shrugged. "I dreamed of you," he said.
sentences.grammar: The short, plain sentence lands hard after the long buildup ('a dozen quips… each crueler'); its very simplicity signals that this, at last, is the truth.
sentences.simple: Asked why he came back for Brienne, Jaime drops all his cruel jokes and gives the one honest answer: he dreamed of her — in the dream they stood together against the darkness.

sentences.context: "No more than Theon Greyjoy would harm Bran or Rickon?"
sentences.grammar: A cutting rhetorical question: Catelyn answers Robb's claim ('Jon would never harm my sons') with a parallel case that destroys it — 'no more than Theon would harm Bran or Rickon' (and Theon did).
sentences.simple: Catelyn's cruel reply: Robb says Jon would never harm Robb's sons — but Robb also trusted Theon, and Theon supposedly murdered Bran and Rickon. Trust proved worthless before.

sentences.context: the trap he'd planned for Moat Cailin worked as well as the one
sentences.grammar: Ironic parallel: 'the trap he'd planned for Moat Cailin' (for the enemy) is compared with 'the one in which he'd just caught her' (his own mother) — the same cleverness turned on family.
sentences.simple: The irony: Robb has just trapped his own mother — using his royal command to force her to agree to naming Jon heir — as neatly as he plans to trap the ironborn at Moat Cailin. Catelyn hopes the real trap works as well as the one that caught her.

sentences.context: Paul's hands were coal, his face was milk, his eyes shone a bitter blue.
sentences.grammar: Three parallel clauses with omitted 'as' ('hands were coal' = hands were black as coal); the triple beat — coal, milk, bitter blue — paints the wight in black, white, and cold blue.
sentences.simple: Three stark images describe the wight: hands black as coal, face white as milk, eyes glowing a cold bitter blue.

sentences.context: Only when he grasped the offered hand did he realize that the rider
sentences.grammar: 'Only when…' front-loads the time clause for suspense; the horror lands in the flat, factual follow-up — 'His hand was black and cold' — stated without any scream or exclamation.
sentences.simple: The chill reveal: only when Sam takes the rider's hand does he realize the rescuer wears no glove — his hand is black and cold, with fingers hard as stone. Their savior is dead himself, like the wights.

sentences.context: "For three dragons I should own the bloody ferry."
sentences.grammar: Hyperbole (wild exaggeration) as complaint: 'for X I should own Y' is a formula for saying a price is absurd — the price named would buy the whole business.
sentences.simple: The Hound's hyperbole: the ferryman's price is so outrageous that for three gold dragons he should own the ferry itself, not just buy one crossing.

sentences.context: I'm as much a commander as we have now. The meanest of the cripples.
sentences.grammar: Self-deprecating humor: 'the meanest of the cripples' — 'mean' here means tough/lowly, not unkind; Noye, a cripple himself, claims command as the best of a broken lot.
sentences.simple: Donal Noye's grim joke: with all the real officers dead or missing, he — a one-armed smith — is as much a commander as Castle Black has left. He is the toughest ('meanest') of the crippled men remaining.

sentences.context: "We'll have music, such sweet music, and wine, heh, the red will run,
sentences.grammar: Ominous double meaning: 'the red will run' reads as 'red wine will flow,' but 'red' also means blood — dramatic irony, since the audience fears the Red Wedding the characters cannot see coming.
sentences.simple: Walder Frey promises music, wine, 'the red will run' — it sounds like red wine flowing freely, but it darkly hints that blood will flow. The reader hears the threat; Catelyn does not.

sentences.context: She's a maid on the eve of her wedding. A few tears
sentences.grammar: Dramatic irony: Catelyn reads Roslin's tears innocently (wedding nerves), while the reader — primed by 'the red will run' — suspects she weeps because she knows the wedding is a trap.
sentences.simple: Catelyn reassures Edmure that Roslin's tears are normal — a maid weeping on her wedding eve. The dramatic irony: the reader fears Roslin is crying because she knows what the Freys plan to do at the wedding.

sentences.context: So long as he kept his eyes down you could not see his face
sentences.simple: If he kept looking down, no one could see his face — only the whites of his eyes.
sentences.grammar: 'So long as' means 'if'; it sets the condition for the main clause.

sentences.context: And under the roughspun was boiled leather and oiled mail
sentences.simple: Under the rough farm clothes, Arya knew, he was wearing boiled leather and oiled chain mail.
sentences.grammar: The word order is flipped for emphasis: the subject 'boiled leather and oiled mail' comes after the verb 'was'.

sentences.context: it took several moments for the team to pull them free again
sentences.simple: The horses needed several moments to pull the wheels out of the deep mud.
sentences.grammar: 'It took [time] for [someone] to [do something]' tells how long an action needed.

sentences.context: There was nothing between her and her mother but a castle gate
sentences.simple: Only a castle gate, a river, and an army stood between her and her mother.
sentences.grammar: 'Nothing but X' means 'only X' — here it lists the last three things keeping them apart.

sentences.context: I heard all about that, don't think I didn't, heh
sentences.simple: Be sure that I heard all about it.
sentences.grammar: The double negative 'don't think I didn't' is used for strong emphasis: it means 'I certainly did.'

sentences.context: Might be you're king, I won't say you're not
sentences.simple: You may be king — I won't deny it — but under my roof, my rules hold.
sentences.grammar: Words are left out: 'It might be that you're king.' Walder means Robb's crown means nothing in his hall.

sentences.context: The lad has a third his capacity, what did he expect
sentences.simple: The boy can only drink a third of what the Greatjon can, so of course he lost the drinking contest.
sentences.grammar: 'Has a third his capacity' means 'can hold only a third as much drink'; the question is sarcastic.

sentences.context: as well as snails might suit a bowl of porridge
sentences.simple: The music suited the song's words not at all — as badly as snails would suit porridge.
sentences.grammar: Sarcastic 'as well as': it claims a good fit but means the fit is terrible.

sentences.context: she was not like to be a stranger to the custom
sentences.simple: With so many siblings, she was not likely to be unfamiliar with the bedding custom.
sentences.grammar: Old use of 'like to' meaning 'likely to': 'was not like to be' = 'was not likely to be.'

sentences.context: you are become an old silly woman sick with grief
sentences.simple: You have become an old silly woman, sick with grief and fear.
sentences.grammar: Old perfect form: 'are become' means 'have become.'

sentences.context: If it pleases Lord Walder to serve me stewed crow
sentences.simple: Robb said he would suffer any insult from Lord Walder — even shameful humiliation — and ask for more.
sentences.grammar: 'Stewed crow' plays on the idiom 'eat crow,' to suffer shame; the 'if' sentence shows how far Robb would go to stay polite.

sentences.context: Only maybe it wasn't her ears that heard it
sentences.simple: Perhaps she did not really hear it with her ears; she felt it in her body, sharp with rage and grief.
sentences.grammar: 'Only' here means 'except' — the sentence suggests the howl reached her some way other than hearing.

sentences.context: where the man had sat only a steel dog remained
sentences.simple: When he put on the helm, he no longer looked like a man — only a steel snarling dog remained.
sentences.grammar: Poetic flipped word order: the subject 'only a steel dog' comes last, for a startling effect.

sentences.context: The black sky wept, the river grumbled, men cursed and died
sentences.simple: It rained, the river made angry sounds, and men were cursing and dying.
sentences.grammar: Three short parallel clauses give nature human actions — weeping, grumbling — to match the dying men.

sentences.context: she ran from him as Mycah must have run
sentences.simple: She ran the way Mycah surely ran when the Hound chased him down.
sentences.grammar: 'As' compares her running to Mycah's; 'must have run' means 'surely ran.'

sentences.context: I have Joffrey and my sister to displease me
sentences.simple: Joffrey, my sister, my father, and three hundred Dornishmen are already upsetting me.
sentences.grammar: 'Have + person + to + verb' means that person does the verb to me: Joffrey displeases me.

sentences.context: the more Tyrion tried to make sense of his accounts
sentences.simple: The harder Tyrion tried to understand the accounts, the more his head ached.
sentences.grammar: 'The more X, the more Y' means: as X grows, Y grows with it.

sentences.context: to talk of breeding dragons instead of locking them up in the treasury
sentences.simple: It is easy to praise Littlefinger's idea of investing gold instead of locking it away.
sentences.grammar: 'Breeding dragons' is a joke: gold coins are called dragons, so 'breeding' them means making money grow by investing.

sentences.context: wouldn't have been so quick to let Joffrey fling
sentences.simple: If I had known the Antler Men owed money to the crown, I would not have let Joffrey kill them so fast.
sentences.grammar: 'Wouldn't have been so quick to' looks back with regret: he wishes he had hesitated.

sentences.context: meant to mine the Mountain for every last nugget of ore
sentences.simple: Tywin planned to squeeze every bit of use out of Gregor before handing him to the Dornish for punishment.
sentences.grammar: 'Mine' is used as a verb meaning 'dig all the value out of'; 'turn over' means 'hand over.'

sentences.context: I could have your tongue out for saying that
sentences.simple: I could have your tongue torn out for saying that.
sentences.grammar: 'Have + object + past participle' means 'cause it to be done': have your tongue (torn) out.

sentences.context: with a courtesy so cold it was like to freeze their ears off
sentences.simple: He spoke so coldly and politely that it felt freezing.
sentences.grammar: Old 'be like to' means 'be likely to': his courtesy was likely to freeze their ears off.

sentences.context: Wars are won with quills and ravens, wasn't that what you said
sentences.simple: Didn't you say wars are won by scheming and messages, not by fighting?
sentences.grammar: 'Quills and ravens' stand for writing letters and sending messages — the tools of plotting.

sentences.context: with what secret messages I never knew
sentences.simple: Ravens and riders carried secret messages, but I never knew what they said.
sentences.grammar: The object is fronted for style: normal order would be 'I never knew with what secret messages.'

sentences.context: it was in Aerys to murder Jaime, with no more cause than spite
sentences.simple: Aerys was the kind of man who would murder Jaime out of pure spite.
sentences.grammar: 'It was in X to do Y' is an old way to say 'X was capable of doing Y.'

sentences.context: The wolf leaves no heirs, the kraken too many
sentences.simple: Robb Stark died with no heir, but Balon Greyjoy left too many heirs.
sentences.grammar: Words are left out: 'The wolf leaves no heirs; the kraken leaves too many [heirs].'

sentences.context: The red woman was all Selyse was not
sentences.simple: Melisandre was young, full-bodied, and strangely beautiful — everything Selyse was not.
sentences.grammar: 'All X was not' means 'everything that X was not.'

sentences.context: I know little of dragons and less of gods
sentences.simple: I know almost nothing about dragons, and even less about gods.
sentences.grammar: 'Less' here means 'even less': he knows little of dragons and still less of gods.

sentences.context: You are short a king, my lady
sentences.simple: You are missing one king — two dead kings do not make three.
sentences.grammar: 'Short' means 'missing': Davos says the leeches account for only two deaths, not three.

sentences.context: the higher a man climbs the farther he has to fall
sentences.simple: The more powerful you become, the worse your fall when you fail.
sentences.grammar: 'The higher X, the farther Y': as the first grows, so does the second — a proverb pattern.

sentences.context: Only a starving man begs bread from a beggar
sentences.simple: Only the truly desperate ask for help from someone who has nothing to give.
sentences.grammar: A proverb: a short wise saying stating a general truth.

sentences.context: he was the King of the Painted Table
sentences.simple: People called Stannis king, but really he ruled nothing except his map table.
sentences.grammar: 'In name' means 'in title only'; the Painted Table is his map — so he is king of a map, not a kingdom.

sentences.context: Well, ravens might have wings, but lords and kings do not
sentences.simple: Ravens can fly fast, but lords and kings cannot — so no help would arrive today.
sentences.grammar: A balanced contrast: 'ravens might have wings' against 'lords and kings do not [have wings].'

sentences.context: There's nothing half so mortal as a grey goose feather
sentences.simple: Nothing is nearly as deadly as an arrow with a grey goose feather.
sentences.grammar: 'Nothing half so mortal as X' means 'nothing nearly as deadly as X'; 'mortal' here means 'deadly.'

sentences.context: like trying to pull a left boot on your right foot
sentences.simple: Entering Hodor's mind felt wrong and difficult, like wearing the wrong boot.
sentences.grammar: A simile explains the difficulty: forcing his mind into Hodor's is like forcing the wrong boot on.

sentences.context: the boot was scared too, the boot didn't know what was happening
sentences.simple: Hodor's mind was frightened and fought back against Bran.
sentences.grammar: 'The boot' means Hodor's body and mind — Bran feels Hodor's own fear pushing him away.

sentences.context: There are old sellswords and bold sellswords, but no old bold sellswords
sentences.simple: Sellswords who take bold risks don't live to grow old.
sentences.grammar: A proverb in three balanced parts: old soldiers survive precisely by not being bold.

sentences.context: The crow calls the raven black, and you speak of betrayal
sentences.simple: You accuse me of betrayal, but you are a traitor yourself.
